Summary: THE PILOT WAS ATTEMPTING A GLASSY WATER LANDING IN A WHITEOUT CONDITION CAUSED BY SMOKE FROM FOREST FIRES. THE AIRCRAFT STRUCK THE WATER AND OVERTURNED. THE AIRCRAFT WAS NOT EQUIPPED WITH AN ARTIFICIAL HORIZON AND DID NOT HAVE A VALID CERTIFICATE OF AIRWORTHINESS.

A78P0069: THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED FROM THE SQUAMISH AIRPORT AT APPROXIMATELY 1915 PST ON A LOCAL PLEASURE FLIGHT WITH THE POSSIBILITY OF LOOKING FOR ACCESS ROADS TO SNOWMOBILING AREAS. THE AIRCRAFT WAS OBSERVED ON TAKE-OFF TO USE MORE RUNWAY THAN NORMAL. AT APPROXIMATELY 1925 PST A "BIRD DOG" INVESTIGATING A FOREST FIRE REPORTED SEEING REMAINS OF AN AIRCRAFT IN THE FIRE. THE AIRCRAFT HAD BEEN FLYING TOWARDS RISING TERRAIN WHEN THE LEFT WING STRUCK A TREE AND WAS TORN OFF AT THE WING ROOT. THE CABIN SECTION WAS CONSUMED BY A POST-IMPACT FIRE. WEATHER CONDITIONS WERE GOOD FOR VFR FLIGHT. THE AIRCRAFT WAS ESTIMATED TO BE AT OR ABOVE ALL UP WEIGHT AT THE TIME OF THE CRASH. THE WEIGHT COMBINED WITH THE HIGH AMBIENT TEMPERATURES AT 3300' ALTITUDE WOULD REDUCE AIRCRAFT CLIMB PERFORMANCE. ALTHOUGH THE ACTUAL CAUSE IS UNDETERMINED; THE CIRCUMSTANCES ARE CONSISTENT WITH THE FACT THAT THE AIRCRAFT WOULD HAVE DIFFICULTY OUTCLIMBING THE RISING TERRAIN.

A78P0093: AFTER DELAYING DUE TO POOR WEATHER THE PILOT WITH 4 PASSENGERS AND FREIGHT DEPARTED FROM DRAGON LAKE ON A CHARTER FLIGHT TO ANOTHER LAKE ABOUT 65 MILES TO THE EAST. THE PILOT CALLED 30 MINUTES LATER AND STATED THAT HE WOULD BE LATE RETURNING BECAUSE OF WEATHER. THE BURNING WRECKAGE WAS LOCATED SOME HOURS LATER BY A RANGER INVESTIGATING A REPORTED FOREST FIRE. INVESTIGATION REVEALED THAT AT TAKE-OFF THE AIRCRAFT WAS 359 LBS OVERWEIGHT, AND THE C OF G WAS 1.5 INCHES AFT OF THE AFT LIMIT. AFTER 45 MINUTES OF FLIGHT THE AIRCRAFT WOULD BE 200 LBS OVERWEIGHT, AND THE C OF G WOULD BE 0.5 INCH AFT OF THE LIMIT. WEATHER IN THE AREA WAS INFLUENCED BY AN UPPER TROUGH WITH A MOIST AND STABLE AIR MASS. WEATHER OBSERVED BY RESIDENTS AND TRUCKERS INDICATED LOW CEILING AND VISIBILITY, WITH FOG OBSCURING SOME HILLS. VFR FLIGHT COULD NOT BE SUCCESSFULLY CARRIED OUT IN THE CONDITIONS DESCRIBED. AN AIRCRAFT, LIKELY THE ACCIDENT AIRCRAFT, WAS SEEN FLYING WEST NEAR THE ACCIDENT SITE 40 TO 45  MINUTES AFTER TAKE-OFF. DENSE BLACK SMOKE WAS REPORTED BY A TRUCKER TRAVELLING THROUGH THE AREA 10 TO 15 MINUTES AFTER THE SIGHTINGS. THE AIRCRAFT HAD STRUCK TREES WHILE INVERTED IN A NOSE LOW, WINGS LEVEL ATTITUDE WITH A HIGH RATE OF DESCENT. A SEVERE POST-IMPACT FIRE DESTROYED THE CABIN OF THE AIRCRAFT. IT IS CONCLUDED THAT THE PILOT LOST CONTROL IN INSTRUMENT CONDITIONS.

THE STUDENT PILOT WAS ON A SOLO FLIGHT WITH INSTRUCTIONS TO REMAIN IN THE VALLEY. INSTEAD HE ELECTED TO FLY TOWARDS HIGHER TERRAIN IN THE AREA OF A FOREST FIRE, WHERE A BIRD-DOG AIRCRAFT HAD CRASHED SEVERAL DAYS EARLIER. HE ENTERED THE SAME VALLEY AND ATTEMPTED TO OUTCLIMB THE RAPIDLY RISING TERRAIN. THE AIRCRAFT EVENTUALLY COLLIDED WITH TREES.

THE PILOT HAD JUST COMPLETED A CHECK FOR A FOREST FIRE AND WAS CLIMBING AWAY WHEN HIS HELICOPTER EXPERIENCED A POWER LOSS. HE AUTOROTATED INTO THE TREES BELOW. THE HELICOPTER WAS SUBSTANTIALLY DAMAGED. SUBSEQUENT INVESTIGATION REVEALED FAILURE OF THE FIRST STAGE PLANETARY GEAR SYSTEM IN THE TRANSMISSION.

A81C0041: AS THE WATER BOMBER PROBE WAS LOWERED BY THE CO-PILOT AT ABOUT 75 KTS, THE AIRCRAFT SWUNG VIOLENTLY LEFT. THE RUN WAS ABORTED WHILE THE MACHINE TURNED 90 DEG AND SINCE WATER WAS SEEN IN THE NOSE COMPARTMENT THE CAPTAIN ELECTED TO BEACH THE AIRCRAFT. ROCKS AND A STEEP BANK ON THE SHORELINE MADE SUCCESSFUL BEACHING IMPOSSIBLE AND THE AIRCRAFT SANK AFTER THE CREW EVACUATED.  THE LEFT NOSEWHEEL DOOR HAD TORN OFF AND WAS THE PROBABLE CAUSE OF THE UNCONTROLLABLE SWING.

A81P0077:  THE PILOT WAS PERFORMING A WATERBOMBING DEMONSTRATION USING A NEWLY CONSTRUCTED 600 GALLON MONSOON BUCKET. AFTER PARTIALLY FILLING THE BUCKET IN A MOUNTAIN LAKE AT THE 4500 FT LEVEL, HE STARTED DOWN THE MOUNTAIN SLOPE AT 60 TO 70 KTS TOWARD THE FIRE AREA. A SHORT TIME LATER, A LOUD BANG WAS HEARD AND THE A/C STARTED TO SHAKE AND YAW TO THE RIGHT. THE BUCKET HAD FLOWN UP AND STRUCK THE TAILBOOM, SEPARATING THE GEAR BOX AND ROTOR FROM THE A/C. THE PILOT FLEW THE HELICOPTER SEVEN MILES FURTHER DOWN THE SLOPE BEFORE MAKING A FORCED LANDING INTO THE TREES. INVESTIGATION SHOWED THAT THE STAINLESS STEEL BAND SECURING THE BOTTOM OF THE BUCKET HAD FAILED, RESULTING IN INSTANTANEOUS LOSS OF THE WATER. THE BOTTOM OPEN, THE BUCKET STREAMED LIKE A DROGUE AND STRUCK THE TAIL. THE PILOT HAD NOT CHECKED THAT THE BUCKET HAD BEEN INSTALLED WITH ATTACHMENT CABLES SEVEN FEET LONGER THAN NORMAL FOR HIS A/C. THE FAILED LOWER BAND WAS NOT RECOVERED; HOWEVER, EXAMINATION OF THE UPPER BAND  SHOWED EVIDENCE OF POOR MANUFACTURING TECHNIQUES THAT WOULD WEAKEN THE ASSEMBLY. IF SIMILAR WORKMANSHIP HAD BEEN EMPLOYED THROUGHOUT, THE LOWER BAND WOULD HAVE BURST WITH THE ADDITION OF THE LOAD OF WATER.

DURING FIRE FIGHTING OPERATIONS, THE PILOT WAS FILLING A WATER BUCKET FROM A SMALL POND. AS HE FLEW AWAY, THE BUCKET APPARENTLY SNAGGED AND HE WAS UNABLE TO JETTISON THE LOAD; THE HELICOPTER WENT OUT OF CONTROL AND ROLLED ON ITS SIDE INTO THE POND. THE SAME PILOT HAD SUCCESSFULLY COMPLETED NUMEROUS WATER PICK-UPS AT THE SAME POND WITHOUT DIFFICULTY. INVESTIGATION REVEALED TWO ITEMS WHICH MAY HAVE CONTRIBUTED TO THE ACCIDENT. THE POND CONTAINED A LARGE AMOUNT OF DEBRIS, INCLUDING SOME OLD CARS, AND THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE WATER BOMBING FLIGHTS, THE GROUND FIRE FIGHTERS WERE ALSO PUMPING WATER OUT OF THE POND NEARBY LOWERING THE WATER LEVEL NEAR THE HIDDEN DEBRIS. THE PILOT WAS MILITARY-QUALIFIED IN THE BELL 212. HIS ATTEMPT TO JETTISON THE BUCKET MAY HAVE BEEN UNSUCCESSFUL AS THE JETTISON BUTTON IN THE 206 IS IN A DIFFERENT POSITION THAN THE 212. IT IS POSSIBLE HE REVERTED TO HIS PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE IN REACTING TO THIS EMERGENCY.

WHILE ON A FLIGHT FROM WATSON LAKE, YUKON, TO FORT NELSON, BC, THE HOMEBUILT A/C BROKE UP. WITNESSES ON THE GROUND REPORTED HEARING AN A/C FLYING OVERHEAD, FOLLOWED BY AN EXPLOSION-LIKE NOISE. AN AIR SEARCH LOCATED PORTIONS OF THE A/C SCATTERED ALONG A 3 MI WRECKAGE PATH. THE SEARCH WAS SEVERELY HAMPERED BY DENSE BUSH AND LOW VISIBILITY CAUSED BY SMOKE FROM A DISTANT FOREST FIRE; TO DATE, SUBSTANTIAL PORTIONS OF THE A/C HAVE NOT BEEN LOCATED. THE FAILURE TO LOCATE MUCH OF THE WING MADE IT DIFFICULT TO DETERMINE THE BREAK-UP SEQUENCE. EVIDENCE SUGGESTS THE WING FAILED BY DOWNWARD BENDING AS A RESULT OF HIGH NEGATIVE "G" LOADS - INDICATIVE OF FAILURE OF THE HORIZONTAL TAIL. EVIDENCE ALSO SUGGESTS THE VERTICAL FIN AND RUDDER SEPARATED EARLY IN THE BREAK-UP SEQUENCE. ALL FRACTURE SURFACES EXAMINED WERE CONSISTENT WITH OVERLOAD FAILURE; THERE WAS NO EVIDENCE OF PRE-CRACKING OR PROGRESSIVE FAILURE. THE WEATHER AT THE TIME OF THE OCCURENCE WAS REPORTEDLY BELOW VFR. SMOKE HAD  REDUCED VISIBILITY TO ABOUT 1/4 MILE. OTHER PILOTS FLYING IN THE AREA REPORTED WIND GUSTING TO 40 KTS WITH MODERATE MECHANICAL TURBULENCE. THESE CONDITIONS, COUPLED WITH THE PILOT'S LACK OF INSTRUMENT FLYING EXPERIENCE AND THE THORP T-18'S SENSITIVE FLIGHT CONTROLS, COULD HAVE LED TO OVERCONTROLLING OR A LOSS OF CONTROL. THIS, IN TURN COULD HAVE RESULTED IN EXCEEDING THE DESIGN LIMITS FOR THE A/C, AND STRUCTURAL FAILURE. EYEWITNESSES REPORTED THE A/C LANDED VERY HEAVILY IN WATSON LAKE. EXAMINATION OF THE LANDING GEAR LEGS REVEALED THEY WERE BOTH BENT OUTWARDS AND TO THE REAR. THESE BENDS WERE NOT THE RESULT OF THE ACCIDENT AS THE LANDING GEAR ASSEMBLY STRUCK THE GROUND INVERTED. RATHER, IT IS POSSIBLE THE BENDING RESULTED FROM THE HARD LANDING. IF SO, SOME FORM OF UNNOTICED STRUCTURAL DAMAGE MAY HAVE OCCURRED DURING THE LANDING THAT LED TO A FAILURE IN FLIGHT. INVESTIGATORS DETERMINED THE A/C WAS NOT BUILT TO THE SPECIFICATIONS AND STANDARDS REQUIRED BY THE DESIGNER. A  NUMBER OF ENGINEERING DRAWINGS HAD NOT BEEN COMPLIED WITH, AND NUMEROUS MODIFICATIONS CONSIDERED CRITICAL BY THE DESIGNER WERE NOT INCORPORATED. THESE INCLUDED STRENGTHENING OF THE MAIN TAIL PLANE SPAR AND MODIFICATIONS TO THE MASS BALANCE WEIGHTS TO REDUCE THE PROBABILITY OF FLUTTER. INVESTIGATORS CONCLUDED THE A/C WAS NOT AIRWORTHY AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT AND THE BREAK-UP MOST PROBABLY WAS THE RESULT OF THE BUILDER'S FAILURE TO ADHERE TO DESIGNER SPECIFICATIONS. IT IS PROBABLE THE INITIAL FAILURE WAS CAUSED BY FLUTTER, AND IT IS POSSIBLE THAT THE BREAK-UP WAS INFLUENCED BY THE PREVAILING WEATHER AND THE EARLIER HARD LANDING. LP 333/82

THE PILOT SIMULATING A FIRE-FIGHTING OPERATION USING A SLING AND MONSOON BUCKET. AFTER A SUCCESSFUL DROP HE RETURNED TO THE LAKE FOR MORE WATER. OVER THE LAKE THE MONSOON BUCKET OR SLING STRUCK A POWER CABLE STRUNG OVER THE LAKE. THE HELICOPTER WAS APPARENTLY BROUGHT TO A SUDDEN STOP, AND AS A RESULT, THE MAIN ROTOR BLADE SEVERED THE TAIL BOOM. THE HELICOPTER FELL TO THE WATER AND SUBMERGED INVERTED. BEFORE HE COULD BE RESCUED, THE PILOT DROWNED. THERE WAS NO EVIDENCE OF ANY COMPONENT FAILURE TO PREVENT THE SUCCESSFUL CONTINUATION OF THE PRACTICE SESSION. THE WIRE STRIKE WAS PROBABLY THE RESULT OF THE PILOT'S INADEQUATE MONITORING OF HELICOPTER'S ALTITUDE. HE WAS AWARE OF THE WIRES, IN FACT HE HAD WARNED ANOTHER PILOT ABOUT THEM SHORTLY BEFORE THE ACCIDENT.

A84W0045: THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED CALGARY EN ROUTE TO THE MOSSE MOUNTAIN AREA TO CARRY OUT A PRACTICE WATER BOMBING RUN.  UPON REACHING THE PRACTICE AREA, THE PILOT CONTACTED THE BIRD DOG PILOT ON THE FORESTRY FREQUENCY.  AFTER THE INITIAL RADIO CONTACT, NO OTHER TRANSMISSIONS WERE MADE.  WHEN THE PILOT OF A SECOND AIRCRAFT ARRIVED AT THE PRACTICE AREA, HE FOUND THAT THE FIRST AIRCRAFT HAD FAILED TO SHOW UP.  WITNESSES IN THE AREA REPORTED SEING AN AIRCRAFT ON FIRE SPINNING TO THE GROUND.  THE LEFT WING OF THE AIRCRAFT WAS FOUND AT A GAS WELL SITE.  THE REMAINDER OF THE AIRCRAFT CRASHED INTO THE TREES APPROXIMATELY HALF A MILE WEST OF WHERE THE LEFT WING HAD SEPARATED. THE INVESTIGATION DETERMINED THAT THE FAILURE OF THE LEFT WING WAS DUE TO A PROGRESSIVE FATIGUE CRACK IN THE FRONT, LOWER SPAR CAP OF THE LEFT WING.  THE FATIGUE CRACK PROGRESSED FROM A MACHINING GROOVE OR CUT ACROSS THE SPAR CAP APPROXIMATELY ONE-SIXTEENTH OF AN INCH DEEP.  AS THE HISTORY OF THE AIRCRAFT COULD NOT  BE ESTABLISHED, THE ORIGIN OF THE MACHINING CUT COULD NOT BE DETERMINED.  SINCE THE OUTBOARD EDGES OF THE CUT ARE UNDER A RIVETED SECTION OF SKIN, IT IS PROBABLE THAT THE CUT WAS MADE EITHER DURING OVERHAUL OR MANUFACTURE. THE LEFT WING AND OTHER PARTS FOUND AT THE GAS WELL SITE SHOWED NO EVIDENCE OF ANY FIRE DAMAGE, AND NEITHER ENGINE SHOWED ANY SIGN OF AN IN-FLIGHT FIRE.  IT CAN BE CONCLUDED THAT ANY IN-FLIGHT FIRE OCCURRED AFTER THE LEFT WING HAD FAILED. THE INVESTIGATION COULD NOT DEFINITELY DETERMINE WETHER OR NOT THE WING FAILURE WAS PILOT INDUCED.  DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT TESTS SHOW THAT, IN THIS AIRCRAFT TYPE, THERE IS A SEVERE PITCHING-UP MOMENT WHEN THE LOAD IS DUMPED.  THIS PITCHING-UP MOMENT IS INCREASED AS THE AIRCRAFT'S SPEED IS INCREASED AND AS THE AMOUNT OF FLAP IS DECREASED.  IF THE PILOT HAD INADVERTENTLY JETTISONED THE LOAD, THE PITCH-UP MOMENT AND RESULTANT INCREASED G LOADING COULD HAVE CAUSED THE WING FAILURE.  A LABORATORY EXAMINATION OF THE BOMB  DOOR ACTUATORS SHOWED THAT THE DOORS WERE CLOSED AT IMPACT. THE AUTOPSY REVEALED THAT THE PILOT'S BLOOD-ALCOHOL LEVEL AT THE TIME OF THE ACCIDENT WAS 1.1 GRAMS PER LITRE.  ALTHOUGH THIS AMOUNT OF ALCOHOL WOULD HAVE ADVERSELY AFFECTED HIS ABILITY TO FLY THE AIRCRAFT, IT IS NOT POSSIBLE TO DETERMINE WETHER THIS FACT HAD ANY BEARING ON THE CAUSE OF THE ACCIDENT. THE FOLLOWING LABORATORY REPORTS WERE COMPLETED:  LP 246/84 - BOMB DOOR ACTUATORS;  LP 247/84 - DROP SELECTOR SWITCH;  AND LP 249/84 - WING SPAR FAILURE. FINDINGS: CAUSE RELATED: 1.  THE LEFT WING WAS WEAKENED DUE TO A FATIGUE CRACK WHICH INITIATED AT A MACHINING CUT IN THE FACE OF THE FORWARD LOWER SPAR CAP. 2.  THE SEQUENCE OF EVENTS DURING THE FLIGHT, RESULTING IN THE WING FAILURE, COULD NOT BE DEETERMINED. OTHER: 1.  THE PILOT'S BLOOD ALCOHOL LEVEL WAS 1.1 GRAMS PER LITRE.

Apres avoir quitte Charlo (Nouveau-Brunswick) en direction de Sorel, le pilote rencontre pour une deuxieme journee consecutive des conditions meteorologiques defavorables. La veille, il etait revenu atterrir a Charlo, mais cette fois-ci il continue vers sa destination. En cours de route, il tente en vain a plusieurs reprises de communiquer avec la station d'information de vol (FSS) de Mont-Joli. Apres environ une heure de vol, les conditions continuent a se deteriorer. Le pilote decide d'effectuer une approche en campagne dans un champs avoisinant. A l'atterrissage, la roulette de nez s'embourbe, l'oleo brise et l'appareil glisse une centaine de pieds avant de s'immobiliser. L'enquete a revele qu'avant son depart, le pilote avait recu un expose meteorologique complet a la station d'information de vol (FSS) de Charlo. Generalement, il pouvait s'attendre a des conditions tres variables le long de sa route, avec des plafonds entre 1 000 pieds et 4 000 pieds au-dessus du  niveau de la mer (ASL) et des visibilites reduites jusqu'a un demi-mille par endroits. L'itineraire prevu (Charlo-Quebec-Sorel) traverse une chaine de montagnes orientee N.-E./S.-O. L'elevation moyenne du terrain varie entre 1 200 pieds et 1 800 pieds au-dessus du niveau de la mer (ASL) avec points culminants s'elevant jusqu'a 2 300 pieds au-dessus du niveau de la mer (ASL). Tel que prevu, les conditions se sont deteriorees a mesure que le vol progressait vers l'ouest. Le pilote a quand meme continue croyant qu'il s'agissait d'un phenomene local et esperant que les conditions s'amelioreraient. Par ailleurs, la visibilite reduite et le plafond bas l'ont contraint a descendre pour rester en vol visuel. Puisqu'il survolait une region montagneuse, cette decision lui a cause deux problemes principaux. En premier lieu, il n'a pas pu maintenir une altitude pertinente et securitaire au-dessus du terrain et, par surcroit, la portee de ses communications a diminue  considerablement. Ne pouvant communiquer avec les stations d'information de vol (FSS) environnantes, il n'a pu verifier si, en realite, les conditions allaient s'ameliorer. Lorsque le pilote s'est rendu compte que poursuivre le vol devenait trop dangereux, les conditions s'etaient deteriorees a un point tel qu'il n'osait plus faire demi-tour ou derouter. La seule option possible etait d'effectuer une approche en campagne. Presse par le temps, il a choisi parmi les champs environnants. Malheureusement, le secteur qu'il survolait etait accidente et les champs etaient cahoteux et detrempes. A l'atterrissage, la surface a entraine une deceleration rapide, la roulette de nez s'est embourbee et l'oleo avant n'a pu resister a la charge. CONCLUSIONS Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. Le pilote n'a pas su reconnaitre les dangers associes au survol de regions montagneuses dans des conditions meteorologiques marginales. 2. Le pilote a poursuivi le vol malgre des conditions  meteorologiques qui justifiaient de faire demi-tour ou de derouter beaucoup plus tot. 3. En retardant la prise de decision, le pilote a ete force d'atterrir dans un secteur peu propice. 4. La surface du champ etait trop irreguliere et detrempee pour permettre un atterrissage securitaire. Autres faits etablis: -Neant-

A87Q0012: A garbled radio call led the pilot of an aircraft to investigate a possible aircraft in distress.  The investigating aircraft discovered a small forest fire started by a crashed aircraft.  Both occupants of the downed aircraft were fatally injured.The Canadian Aviation Safety Board determined that the float-equipped aircraft crashed when the pilot was unable to reach a suitable landing area following a complete engine failure at low altitude.

A87C4034: The aircraft was engaged in fire suppression and had just picked up a load of water from a nearby lake, when the pilot felt a severe vibration coming from the left engine. The pilot jettisoned the load, feathered the propeller, and shut down the engine. Only two of three propeller blades feathered, but the pilot was able to return to Thompson and land safely. Since manufacture, the propeller (Hamilton Standard model 43E60) had accumulated 84 hours in service. During disassembly, it was determined that the blade bushing screws and the blade drive pins that secure the blade bushing to the number two (unfeathered) blade, had failed in shear. The blade thrust washer had a radial crack running completely through it. The manufacturer examined the propeller and found the number two blade to be deformed slightly rearward. This varied from the other two blades, and, as there was no evidence of leading edge damage, was indicative of static blade impact. The damage is  typical of a blade struck during towing or service equipment operations; the strike could have occurred at any time prior to this incident. The thrust washer initially cracked at blade impact and eventually the crack propagated completely through the washer. The sharp edges of the crack scraped out an area inside of the barrel arm and caused the thrust washer to jam against the wall. This resulted in enough resistance that the torque required to change blade angle became greater than the shear strength of the blade bushing screws and the blade drive pins. The screws and pins eventually sheared, and the blade bushing separated from the blade. The blade, now independent of the remaining two blades, assumed a different pitch angle which resulted in excessive propeller vibration. CONCLUSIONS: Findings: 1. The number two blade was deformed slightly rearward because of static blade impact. 2. The blade thrust washer cracked at impact and eventually jammed, causing the number  two blade bushing screws and drive pins to shear. 3. The blade bushing separated from the number two blade resulting in a different blade pitch angle and excessive propeller vibration. Causes: The number two propeller blade had previously received static impact damage. L'avion etait utilise dans le cadre d'operations de lutte contre l'incendie et venait de prendre un chargement d'eau d'un lac voisin lorsque le pilote a ressenti de fortes vibrations en provenance du moteur gauche. Il a largue l'eau, a mis l'helice en drapeau et a coupe le moteur. Seulement deux des trois pales se sont mises en drapeau. Le pilote a toutefois pu retourner se poser sans difficulte a Thompson. Depuis sa fabrication, l'helice (Hamilton, modele 43E60) comptait 84 heures de service. Pendant le demontage, on s'est apercu que les vis du coussinet de pale et les ergots d'entrainement de la pale qui fixent le coussinet a la pale numero deux (la pale qui ne s'est pas mise en drapeau) s'etaient rompus sous l'effet du cisaillement. La rondelle de butee de la pale etait completement criquee dans le sens radial. Le fabricant a examine l'helice et s'est rendu compte que la pale numero deux etait legerement deformee vers l'arriere, ce qui n'etait pas le cas des deux  autres pales. Comme le bord d'attaque de la pale n'etait pas endommage, on presume que la pale a recu un coup alors qu'elle etait immobile, sans doute pendant le remorquage de l'avion ou lors de travaux d'entretien. Le coup a pu etre porte n'importe quand avant l'incident. La rondelle de butee a d'abord ete criquee par le coup porte sur la pale. La crique s'est ensuite propagee completement sur toute la rondelle. Les aretes vives de la crique ont egratigne passablement l'interieur du coussinet, et la rondelle a fini par se bloquer sur les parois du coussinet. La resistance est devenue alors suffisante pour que le couple necessaire pour modifier le pas de la pale depasse la resistance au cisaillement des vis du coussinet et des ergots d'entrainement de la pale. Les vis et les ergots ont fini par se rompre sous l'effet du cisaillement, et le coussinet s'est separe de la pale. The pilot was flying at an altitude of about 50 to 75 feet above the water for a retardant drop on a fire burning on an island in Lake LaBerge, Yukon. The aircraft flew through the smoke, and, as it emerged, the left wing struck a pine tree. The flying characteristics of the aircraft were not affected, and the aircraft was flown back to Whitehorse without difficulty. The pilot had been warned by radio of a tree-top that rose above the general height of the trees in the fire area. He noticed one tree-top off to his right as he approached the fire and assumed that it was the one about which he had been warned. The tree struck by the aircraft protruded about 15 feet above the surrounding trees. The altitude at which the aircraft flew for the retardant drop allowed it to clear the trees on the island with the exception of one or two isolated protruding tree-tops. The pilot believed he had the protruding tree-top mentioned in the radio warning in sight. He did not see the  other protruding tree-top ahead of the aircraft because it was obscured by smoke until just before impact. During the retardant run, the pilot did not fly at a sufficient altitude to ensure that the aircraft would clear all obstacles. FINDINGS: Cause Related: 1. The pilot did not see the protruding tree-top because it was obscured by smoke. 2. The pilot flew at an altitude that would just clear the trees because he believed he had located and would miss a protruding tree-top known to be on the island. Other: -Nil- Le pilote volait a une altitude d'environ 50 a 75 pieds au-dessus de l'eau pour epandre un produit ignifuge sur un feu faisant rage sur une ile du lac Laberge (Yukon). L'avion a traverse la fumee et, lorsqu'il en est sorti, l'aile gauche a heurte un pin, ce qui n'a cependant pas modifie les caracteristiques de vol de l'avion; ce dernier a pu rejoindre Whitehorse sans difficulte. Le pilote avait ete averti par radio que la cime d'un arbre depassait la hauteur de la voute des arbres dans la zone ou l'incendie faisait rage. Il a remarque la cime d'un arbre a sa droite au moment ou il approchait de l'incendie, et il a suppose qu'il s'agissait de celui dont on lui avait parle. L'arbre heurte par l'avion depassait les autres d'environ 15 pieds. L'altitude a laquelle l'avion volait pour larguer le produit ignifuge lui permettait d'eviter les arbres de l'ile a l'exception d'un ou deux arbres isoles qui depassaient les autres. Le pilote a cru qu'il voyait la cime mentionnee dans  l'avertissement radio. Il n'a vu l'autre cime devant lui que juste avant l'impact parce qu'elle etait cachee par la fumee. Pendant la passe d'epandage, le pilote n'a pas maintenu une altitude suffisante pour s'assurer que l'avion franchirait tous les obstacles. CONCLUSIONS Faits etablis se rapportant aux causes: 1. Le pilote n'a pas vu la cime d'un arbre qui depassait les autres parce que la fumee la cachait. 2. Le pilote a vole a une altitude qui permettait juste d'eviter les arbres, croyant avoir apercu la cime de l'arbre dont on lui avait parle et qui n'etait pas sur sa trajectoire. Autres faits etablis: -Neant-

The aerial reconnaissance patrol was working during a period of extensive forest-fire activity in Northern Manitoba.  The patrol had been underway for three hours when the aircraft engine suddenly lost power.  The pilot successfully force-landed the aircraft in an open area, incurring only minor damage.  The occupants were evacuated from the site by helicopter.  The site was in the path of an advancing forest fire, and the airframe was substantially damaged by the fire before it could be removed.
A89P0174:  The Cessna 305 Bird dog (C-FTGB) HAD JUST TAKEN OFF WITH GLIDER IN TOW.  AS IT TURNED, The Cessna NOSED DOWN AND SPUN TO THE GROUND.  The GLIDER was RELEASED.

WHILE ON APPROACH TO CALGARY THE CREW OBSERVED A FIRE WARNING ON #2 ENGINE. BOTH FIRE BOTTLES WERE DISCHARGED AND THE ENGINE WAS SECURED. THE CREW  DECLARED AN EMERGENCY AND REQUESTED ERS. THE CONVAIR LANDED WITHOUT INCIDENT AND WAS CHECKED BY FIRE CREWS - NO FIRE FOUND.

C-FTGU, A CESSNA 305C (L-19 BIRDDOG) AIRCRAFT, WAS ON A LOCAL TRAINING FLIGHT WITH AN INSTRUCTOR PILOT AND A PILOT TRAINEE ON BOARD.  THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED THE DEBERT AIRPORT AT 15:20 ADT AND PROCEEDED TO THE TRAINING AREA WITH THE PILOT TRAINEE AT THE CONTROLS.  THE PURPOSE OF THE FLIGHT WAS TO TYPE CHECK THE PILOT TRAINEE ON THE L-19 AIRCRAFT AS WELL AS A CONVERSION FROM TRICYCLE TO CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT.  AFTER CONDUCTING SOME AERIAL WORK IN THE TRAINING AREA THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED TO THE AIRPORT FOR A FULL STOP LANDING.THE WIND AT THE TIME WAS REPORTED TO BE 230 DEGREES AT 5 TO 10 KNOTS.  HOWEVER, RUNWAY 28 WAS SELECTED FOR THE LANDING BECAUSE OF GLIDER OPERATIONS BEING CONDUCTED FROM RUNWAY 23.  WHEN THE AIRCRAFT WAS ON SHORT FINAL THE WINDSOCK WAS OBSERVED TO BE NEARLY LIMP AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS TRACKING DOWN THE EXTENDED CENTRELINE WITH MINIMAL CONTROL INPUT CORRECTIONS.THE AIRCRAFT TOUCHED DOWN 200 FEET FROM THE THRESHOLD, BOUNCED BACK INTO THE AIR, AND THEN REPORTEDLY SETTLED ONTO THE RUNWAY WITH THE WEIGHT DISTRIBUTED CORRECTLY ON THE WHEELS AND TRACKING DOWN THE RUNWAY CENTRELINE.  DURING THE ROLL OUT THE AIRCRAFT STARTED TO DRIFT TO THE LEFT AND THE INSTRUCTOR PILOT FELT CORRECTING PRESSURE ON THE RIGHT RUDDER PEDAL.  HOWEVER, BY THE TIME HE REALIZED THAT NOT ENOUGH RIGHT RUDDER WAS BEING APPLIED AND ATTEMPTED TO ASSIST THE PILOT TRAINEE, THE SWING TO THE LEFT HAD ALREADY DEVELOPED AND HE WAS UNABLE TO PREVENT THE AIRCRAFT FROM GROUND LOOPING.THIS WAS THE PILOT TRAINEE'S FIRST LANDING IN A CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT.  THE INSTRUCTOR PILOT FEELS THAT IT WOULD HAVE BEEN MORE PRUDENT IF THE INTRODUCTION TO CONVENTIONAL LANDING GEAR AIRCRAFT HAD BEEN CARRIED OUT IN AN AIRCRAFT WITH MORE FORGIVING CHARACTISTICS.

A94O0232:  DURING THE AERIAL SPRAY OPERATION THE PILOT FELT RUDDER OPERATION STIFFENING.  MOMENTS LATER BOTH THE RUDDER AND ELEVATORS SEIZED.  THE ONLY CONTROLS AVAILABLE TO THE PILOT WERE THE AILERONS.  THE PEZETEL M-18 DROMADER RETURNED TO KAPUSKASING WITH THE BIRDDOG AIRCRAFT FLYING ALONGSIDE.  THE LANDING WAS UNEVENTFUL AND EMERGENCY SERVICES WERE STANDING BY.  A PRELIMINARY INSPECTION BY THE OPERATOR REVEALED A POSSIBLE FAILURE OF THE REAR SPAR OF THE VERTICAL FIN.

A95Q0010:  UNABLE TO KEEP RUNWAY CENTER LINE, THE PILOT OF THE B747 ABORTED THE TAKE-OFF FROM RUNWAY 29 AT MIRABEL AT 2206Z.  RUNWAY CONDITIONS WERE REPORTED TO BE FAIR AT 100% SNOW, 1/8 OF AN INCH THICK, 20% ICE PATCHES AND A JBI OF .35.  THE WEATHER WAS CEILING 1300 FEET OBSCURRED, VISIBILITY OF 1 1/2 MILE IN LIGHT SNOW AND WINDS WERE CALM.WHILE TAXIING THE PILOT INDICATED TO THE TOWER THAT HE HAD A HOT BRAKE INDICATION AND REQUESTED AN INSPECTION BE DONE AT 2217Z.  THE TOWER ADVISED THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER OF THE REQUEST AT 2218Z.  THE AIRCRAFT TAXIING ON ALPHA STOPPED AT ALPHA 3 INTERSECTION.URGENCE 1 VEHICULE ALREADY ON GOLF TAXIWAY WAS ADVISED AT 2220Z, AND VIA HOTEL AND ALPHA CAME UP FROM THE BACK OF THE B747.  AT 2221Z THE PILOT WAS ADVISED THAT THE INSPECTION VEHICULE WAS EN ROUTE.  AT 2225Z, THE PILOT INQUIRED AGAIN ABOUT AN INSPECTION VEHICULE, UNAWARE THAT URGENCE 1 HAD PARKED BEHIND THE AIRCRAFT AND THAT PERSONNEL WERE ALREADY UNDER THE AIRCRAFT CHECKING OUT THE BRAKES.BECAUSE OF THE PILOT'S SECOND DEMAND FOR AN INSPECTION VEHICULE, THE TOWER ACTIVATED THE CRASH BELL ALERT TO NOTIFY THE FIRE HALL OF THE IMMEDIATE NEED FOR A VEHICULE.  THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER, AWARE THAT THE FIRE CREW WERE ALREADY ON SITE, WAS CONFUSED BY THE CRASH BELL DEMAND FROM THE TOWER.RUNWAY 29 WAS SWEPT AGAIN AND THE B747 DEPARTED MIRABEL AT 2337Z. URGENCE 1 VEHICULE CREW OMITTED TO CONTACT GROUND CONTROL OF THEIR PRESENCE ON THE AIRPORT TAXIWAYS AND THEREFORE THE TOWER WAS UNAWARE THAT URGENCE 1 WAS RESPONDING TO THE B747'S CALL.AS LONG AS FIRE CREW ARE INSIDE THE VEHICULE THEY CAN COMMUNICATE WITH THE TOWER AND WITH THE FLIGHT CREW.  WHEN OUTSIDE THE VEHICULE, THEY CAN ONLY COMMUNICATE WITH THE FIRE HALL DISPATCHER, WHO CAN THEN RELAY THEIR MESSAGE VIA THE TOWER.THE FIRE HALL INTERVENTION PROCEDURE WILL BE REVISED BECAUSE OF THE POTENTIAL DANGER OF FIRE CREWS WORKING IN PROXIMITY OF THE AIRCRAFT WITHOUT THE FLIGHT CREW'S KNOWLEDGE.

A95A0082: A95A0083: THE CREW OF THE CANADIAN MILITARY CL601, MILITARY 144613, DID A GO-AROUND AFTER A HARD LANDING FROM A FLAPLESS APPROACH.  A VISUAL INSPECTION FROM THE GROUND REVEALED A SEVERELY DAMAGED RIGHT MAIN LANDING GEAR WHICH EVENTUALLY SEPARATED FROM THE AIRCRAFT IN FLIGHT.  AN INFLIGHT FIRE STARTED IN THE FUSELAGE AREA NEAR THE MISSING GEAR LOCATION.AN EMERGENCY LANDING WAS CARRIED OUT IN SHEARWATER AND, ON LANDING, THE AIRCRAFT DEPARTED THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE RUNWAY.  A POST INPACT EXPLOSION AND FIRE IN THE CENTRE FUEL TANK WAS QUICKLY EXTINGUISHED BY THE FIRE CREW.THE CREW OF THE AIRCRAFT, WHO SUFFERED FROM BRUISING AND SMOKE INHALATION,  EVACUATED THROUGH THE OVER WING EXITS.THE CANADIAN MILITARY HAVE CONVENED A BOARD OF INQUIRY.

A95C0153:  AIR CANADA 123, A BOEING 767-233, WAS 80 NM NORTH OF WINNIPEG AT FL390, EN ROUTE FROM TORONTO TO EDMONTON, WHEN THE FORWARD CARGO HOLD FIRE INDICATOR ILLUMINATED.  THE CREW ACTIVATED THE CARGO HOLD FIRE EXTINGUISHER SYSTEM (WHICH DIRECTS FIRE RETARDANT INTO BOTH FORWARD AND REAR CARGO HOLDS), AND DIVERTED THE FLIGHT TO WINNIPEG.  THE CREW CARRIED OUT AN UNEVENTFUL LANDING AND STOPPED ON RUNWAY 18, WITH ERS STANDING BY.  MAINTENANCE OPENED AND CHECKED BOTH CARGO HOLDS, AND FOUND NO EVIDENCE OF FIRE.  ALL CARGO AND BAGGAGE WAS REMOVED FROM BOTH CARGO HOLDS, AND THE AIRCRAFT RESUMED THE FLIGHT TO EDMONTON UNDER THE OPERATOR'S M.E.L., WITH THE CARGO HOLD FIRE DETECTION AND SUPPRESSION SYSTEMS INOPERATIVE. A96C0168:  THE CESSNA 337G, C-FIGS, WAS RETURNING FROM AN AERIAL APPLICATION (FORESTRY) BIRD DOG MISSION.  THE PILOT NORMALLY EXTENDS THE LANDING GEAR ON THE DOWNWIND CIRCUIT LEG, BUT ON THIS OCCASION, HE REPORTEDLY FORGOT TO DO SO.  THE PILOT COMPLETED A (POWER-ON) SHORT-FIELD APPROACH TO THE GRAVEL RUNWAY, AND TOUCHED DOWN WITH THE LANDING GEAR RETRACTED.  THE GEAR WARNING HORN REPORTEDLY ACTIVATES WHEN THE POWER IS REDUCED TO IDLE.  NEITHER THE PILOT NOR THE ONE PASSENGER WERE INJURED.  THE AIRCRAFT SUSTAINED DAMAGE TO ITS BELLY AND PROPELLERS.

A97P0207:  The pilot of the Bell 206B helicopter (serial number 478) was engaged in transporting survey crews in the Bear Valley area, about 45 nautical miles (nm) north of Mackenzie, British Columbia. On the morning of the accident, he had begun flying at about 0645 Pacific daylight time (PDT). A survey crew contacted the pilot by radio at about 1200 and requested a pick-up for about 1400; they also informed the pilot of a 100- to 150-foot ceiling and a visibility of about 300 metres (1000 feet). At about 1445, the pilot was attempting to locate the survey crew at the 5100-foot elevation, but low cloud, fog, and precipitation prevented him from making visual contact with the landing area. The pilot was in two-way radio contact with the ground crews and remarked that the lower pick-up pad was fogged in and that he could not see the trees or ground below him. The pilot continued manoeuvring in the area, searching for the landing pad. Witnesses on the ground then saw the helicopter appear from the base of the low cloud, in a right-hand, descending turn, roughly in a 40-degree nose-down and 40-degree right-bank attitude before it struck trees and collided with the terrain at 5200 feet above sea level (asl), inside a cirque. The pilot was fatally injured, and the helicopter was destroyed by impact forces and a post-crash fire.The helicopter was manufactured in 1969, and maintenance records reveal that the helicopter was certificated, equipped, and maintained in accordance with existing regulations and approved procedures. As of 26 July 1997, it had 11 640 hours of flight time, and the Allison 250-C20B engine had 10 003 hours. The helicopter's weight and centre of gravity at the time of the accident are not conclusively known, but based on the day's previous activities, it is estimated that the weight and balance were within the prescribed limits and that there was sufficient fuel on board for the flight.The helicopter struck the rocky surface at a high impact angle and was damaged by an intense post-crash fire, except for the aft section of the tail boom, the tail rotor assembly, two doors, and fragments of the skid gear. No flight or engine instruments were recovered, except for the face of the engine torque gauge. The TSB Engineering Branch examination of this dial did not reveal any impact-related reading. All flight controls were destroyed by impact and fire. The main rotor gearbox and the engine gearbox were also destroyed by fire. An examination of the gears and bearings that remained did not reveal any anomaly or indication of pre-impact distress or malfunction. The aircraft systems were examined to the degree possible, and no sign of a malfunction was found.Four days before the accident, the pilot had experienced smoke in the cockpit resulting from an electrical short circuit in the directional gyro (DG). Company maintenance personnel in Mackenzie removed the DG and inspected the associated wiring loom and cannon plug; the helicopter was then test-flown and returned to the Bear Valley camp without the DG installed. The removal of the DG did not affect the airworthiness of the helicopter. The DG was not required for the pilot to navigate in visual meteorological conditions (VMC), since a magnetic compass was installed in the helicopter as standard equipment. The absence of the DG could have affected the pilot's ability to fly in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). The accident helicopter was not authorized to fly under instrument flight rules (IFR) conditions.Witnesses recalled that when the helicopter departed on this trip, waves of low cloud and fog were moving through the area, and the visibility had diminished to about one mile in drizzle; the sky condition at the drop site was described as a solid overcast around 600 feet above ground level (agl). These weather conditions reportedly persisted throughout the day. Witnesses also reported that there was very little wind at the time of the accident, that light rain was falling, and that the fog and low cloud coming up the slope caused an overcast ceiling of about 300 feet agl. About two hours after the accident, the same weather conditions prevented another helicopter from landing at the accident site. The weather reporting station nearest the accident area is 45 nm away in Mackenzie. At 1300, the automated weather observation system (AWOS) at Mackenzie had recorded a measured ceiling of 700 feet overcast and a visibility of more than 9 miles. At 1400 the sky condition was 500 feet scattered, 1600 feet broken, and 2800 feet overcast, and the visibility was more than 9 miles, in very light drizzle. In the hour between these reports, four special observations recorded a broken ceiling as low as 500 feet. Based on witnesses accounts, however, the weather conditions at the accident site were significantly different from the Mackenzie AWOS. This was likely because of the distance and the mountainous terrain, which is known to create unpredictable local weather conditions.The 45-year-old pilot had recently begun his career in aviation, and had accumulated about 400 hours of total flying time. He held a Canadian commercial helicopter pilot licence (CPL-H), endorsed for the Bell 47 and 206 helicopters, for daylight flying only, and a valid medical certificate. The pilot did not hold an instrument rating, nor was it required, since this operation was to be conducted under visual flight rules (VFR). The pilot had attended a course on pilot decision making in April 1997. His only exposure to instrument flying was during basic training toward his CPL-H.In early May 1997, the pilot had successfully completed the operator's Upgrade Training Program, which included mountain-flying and reduced-visibility training, and his pilot proficiency check. On May 12 he began as a base pilot in Mackenzie, and on July 2 the pilot assumed his duties at the Bear Valley camp. The Bear Valley contract was the pilot's first commercial assignment and his first exposure to remote-base and self-dispatch operations. He was expected to make routine operational decisions involving customer requirements, weather, helicopter serviceability, and the suitability of the terrain, although he could easily consult with the operations bases in Prince George or MacKenzie. On July 7 he experienced a main rotor blade strike during a confined-area approach in the Bear Valley area. The next day, the company chief pilot carried out an evaluation flight and debriefing with him before he returned to the Bear Valley operation and continued his assignment.The pilot had flown about 120 hours in the 30 days before the accident and at least 16 hours in the last 3 days; he was scheduled to begin his time off the following day. An examination of the pilot's flight time/days off records revealed at least 12 instances in the previous 70 days where his flight- and duty-times exceeded the limits specified in the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs Sections 700.16, 720.16, and 720.17 ). During the 30 days before the accident, the pilot did not have the required 8 hours of rest on five occasions and had exceeded the 14-hour duty time limit on eight occasions, the most recent being on the day before the accident.It is apparent from his records that the pilot had been filling in the forms incorrectly. If filled in correctly, these records would have allowed the pilot and the operator to accurately maintain and monitor his flight time and duty time to prevent him from exceeding the daily and cumulative limits specified in the CARs.On 28 April 1992, Transport Canada (TC) conducted a regional audit of Northern Mountain Helicopters Incorporated (NMH) and identified several areas of non-conformance, mainly regarding pilot training records, flight- and duty-time records, and aircraft journey log entries. As a result of this audit, the company pledged to undertake a plan to rectify the areas of concern. TC carried out another in-depth audit of the company between May 11 and May 22, 1998, which focussed on the 18-month period from October 1996 to May 1998. The purpose of the audit was to assess the operator's level of conformance with the regulations and standards governing the operations of Canadian air operators. The results of this 1998 audit noted that significant changes in the company structure and operations following the 1992 audit were insufficient to address all of the noted deficiencies.In the six-year period between the audits, the TC Centre (TCC) in Prince George, British Columbia (B.C.), had carried out maintenance inspections and audits of several NMH bases. These inspections/audits and their results were recorded in the Prince George TCC, but were not forwarded to the TC Pacific Region office in Vancouver, and the 1998 audit did not reflect the Prince George inspections. The inspections carried out by the TCC identified frequent maintenance-related deficiencies; TCC inspectors later assessed most of the company's responses to these findings as satisfactory.Nevertheless, in January 1996 a TCC audit of the NMH aircraft and maintenance facilities identified 17 deficiencies, several of which were recurring since the audit carried out in January 1994. As a result, TC Airworthiness sent a letter to NMH stating that TC was alarmed at the results, and warned that the Approved Maintenance Organization Certificate, number 144-90, would be suspended if the company did not meet the requirements of the letter. The certificate was not suspended at that time.In December 1997, about five months after the accident, TC Pacific Region issued NMH two Notices of Suspension, one each for the Canadian Air Operator Certificate, number 1518, and the Approved Maintenance Organization Certificate, number 144-90, because TC determined that the company had failed to comply with the conditions required for the issuance of these certificates. Following response by NMH to the conditions of the suspensions, TC later withdrew the Notices of Suspension.At the time of the 1998 audit, NMH offered domestic, non-scheduled international, and aerial work air services from the main base at Prince George, B.C., and from eleven sub-bases in B.C., one sub-base in Ontario, and two international operational bases in Sudan and Congo. NMH operated a mixed fleet of about 70 aircraft and held Air Operator Certificate number 1518. The operator employed about 130 pilots and operated under Subparts 702, 703, and 704 of the CARs in diverse flight operations such as general charter, heli-logging, forest fire management, aerial construction, and seismic support.As a result of the 1998 audit, a total of 54 airworthiness findings and 17 operational findings were made, several of which TC assessed would have had an impact on flight safety. TC technical inspectors noted several deficiencies in the areas of technical records, maintenance schedules, defect deferral, maintenance dispatch, and quality assurance. According to TC, the airworthiness findings suggested that the company had less-than-acceptable control over various components on the maintenance system and that, as evidenced by the number and seriousness of the findings, the company had made little effort to comply with all aspects of the (then) new CARs.TC operational inspectors identified several areas of concern resulting from the audit. The most important of these were the lack of effective flight and duty time monitoring, and poorly kept pilot training records. These deficiencies had the potential to adversely affect flight safety. The TC auditors found that the flight crew training program was lacking in several areas, notably in training for flight in reduced visibility. Further, pilot training records were found to have been inaccurate and incomplete. The TC auditors found that the system in place for tracking pilot flight and duty times was extraordinarily inaccurate and ineffective. As well, the auditors made five findings regarding company pilots exceeding the flight- and duty-time limitations contained in the CARs. Three of these findings concerned the accident pilot: he had less than the required minimum rest periods on five occasions; he had duty time in excess of the maximum on five occasions; and he had been given only two days of rest in the 31-day period before the accident (OP-09-01 to OP-09-03).In partial summary, the audit revealed the following about the operator:	1.	the maintenance control system did not comply with Commercial Air Service Standards;	2.	company aircraft were not maintained in accordance with an effective maintenance control system that met the requirements of CAR Part VII - Commercial Air Services, Subpart 6 - Aircraft Maintenance Requirements for Air Operators;	3.	pilots had not completed the required ground- and flight-training programs;	4.	the system to monitor flight time, duty time, and rest periods was not followed; and,	5.	each pilot was not provided with the required time free from duty.On 4 June 1998, as a result of this audit, TC issued the operator a Notice of Suspension under Section 7.1(1)(b) of the Aeronautics Act, effective 8 June 1998. To avoid further action against the operator's Air Operator Certificate, TC required the operator to comply with the conditions specified in the Notice of Suspension within 30 days. On 8 June 1998, a Special Inspection Team from TC examined the operator's compliance with the conditions. In summary, TC found that the operator had "co-operated on all levels with a clear understanding of deficiencies identified." As well, TC noted that "steps were already being taken to correct deficiencies and prevent future occurrence." Accordingly, the Notice of Suspension was withdrawn.Nevertheless, the operator's responses to the operational finding concerning the accident pilot (OP-09-01 to 03) were all assessed as unacceptable by TC in July 1998. The TC inspector noted that the operator's responses put into question the operator's grasp of the flight- and duty-time limitations. The inspector also noted that more was needed to educate the flight crews about flight and duty times and to enforce the limitations of the CARs. TC has continued to monitor the operator since that time and has assessed as satisfactory the operator's response to each deficiency noted since.Fatigue is a debilitating phenomenon which slows reaction time, reduces concentration, and can lead to errors of attention. The performance and judgement of an individual suffering from fatigue becomes degraded, and one common effect is an increase in that individual's willingness to take risks and a tendency to finish tasks more quickly. The two most common causes are insufficient rest and a lack of sleep. Research shows that, although individual needs vary, the majority of the population requires between 7.5 and 8.5 hours of sleep in a 24-hour period. If people obtain less than their requirement, they develop a sleep debt, which is cumulative. This occurs when insufficient quantity of sleep continues over several consecutive days. For example, missing one hour of sleep per day for four days has about the same effect as missing fours hours of sleep in one night. Furthermore, the impact of sleep debt is compounded when it is combined with a long day.On the ground, spatial orientation is sensed by the combination of vision, muscle sense, and specialized organs in the inner ear, which sense linear and angular accelerations. Vision is the strongest of the orienting senses, and in visual flight, the pilot relies on regular visual references with the ground and horizon to control the aircraft attitude and altitude. If a pilot is in cloud, the visual reference to the ground and horizon is lost. As a result, the available cues (solely from the external forces on the body) often produce spatial disorientation in flight, because the pilot has a false impression of aircraft attitude and motion. Under these conditions, the pilot is completely dependent on the flight instruments and learned flying skills for control of the aircraft. Inexperienced pilots with little instrument time are particularly susceptible to spatial disorientation when they are confronted with no external visual attitude references. Without suitable flight instruments or skills, a disoriented pilot would quickly lose control of the aircraft. Research found in the FAA Advisory Circular 60-4A, shows that a pilot can take as long as 35 seconds to re-establish full control of an aircraft by using instruments alone. In that period, the pilot spends at least five seconds recognizing that a hazard exists, determining the necessary corrective action, and responding to it. Instrument flight training in itself does not prevent disorientation, rather it provides the pilot with the ability to overcome it.The pilot may have decided to attempt the crew pick-up in adverse weather conditions because of his reluctance to leave the survey crews stranded and his desire to do well in his first unsupervised assignment. His assessment of the potential risks involved may have been influenced by his limited experience.The survey crews saw the helicopter emerge from the low clouds in an extreme flight attitude, which was not consistent with controlled flight in this type of helicopter. The crews' description of the brief flight path before impact, as well as wreckage and impact characteristics, indicate that the pilot had insufficient time or altitude to prevent the collision with the terrain. Such a loss of control most likely was the result of spatial disorientation.While the possibility exists that a mechanical malfunction did occur, no definitive conclusions about the mechanical condition of the helicopter can be drawn from the available wreckage. The remainder of the analysis will focus on the possible human performance aspects of this accident.The absence of the DG, while not affecting the pilot's ability to navigate in VMC, could have limited his ability to maintain control in IMC. Although the weather conditions reported by ground observers were not consistent with VMC, the actual in-flight conditions experienced by the pilot are not conclusively known. It is probable the pilot encountered the same conditions as those that were observed and that, as a result, he rapidly became disoriented.The pilot had, on occasion, exceeded the limitations concerning flight time, duty time, and rest periods. As well, several days before the accident, he had entered into a period when, although individuals can vary, the average person would have experienced serious cumulative sleep debt. Although the pilot recorded a normal sleep period immediately before the day of the accident, it is possible that the effect of the recent sleep debt may have adversely affected his performance or decision-making ability. It could not be determined if fatigue-related factors contributed to the circumstances of this accident; nonetheless, the workload and schedule of the pilot included periods when the risk of fatigue-related performance decrements would have been elevated.TC audit findings show that the operator had not exercised effective operational control of the company's maintenance and operational activities. In particular, the method for tracking pilot flight and duty time was ineffective and inaccurate. This allowed the accident pilot to exceed the maxima, and it prevented the operator from monitoring and regulating the pilot appropriately. Such lack of operational control and administrative support may have increased the burden of workload on the accident pilot, perhaps exacerbating his overall stress and fatigue levels and diminishing his judgement.The TC audit of the company in 1992 revealed several areas of non-conformance, and the company pledged to rectify the areas of concern. However, it was not until the regulatory audit from 11 to 22 May 1998, following this occurrence, that TC carried out another audit of the company.TC issued repeated warnings of suspension of the company's maintenance and operational activities during the period between the audits, ultimately precipitating the most recent Notice of Suspension of the Air Operator Certificate in June 1998. Following the 1992 Transport Canada audit, deficiencies related to the company's air operator certificate and the approved maintenance organization certificate, were either not eliminated or were allowed to re-emerge.1.	The weather in the vicinity of the accident made it unlikely that the flight could be completed in visual meteorological conditions.2.	The helicopter emerged from the low cloud base in a steep, nose-down turn, and there was insufficient altitude and time to prevent the aircraft from striking the ground.3. 	The pilot likely experienced spatial disorientation and lost control of the helicopter.1.	The pilot's work/rest schedule increased the probability of him making fatigue-related errors in both aircraft handling and judgement.2.	According to the company records, the pilot had, on several occasions, exceeded the legislated flight- and duty-time limitations of the CARs.3.	Transport Canada audits carried out after the accident revealed deficiencies in the company's control of maintenance and operational activities.4.	Following the 1992 Transport Canada audit, deficiencies related to the company's air operator certificate and the approved maintenance organization certificate, were either not eliminated or were allowed to re-emerge.5.	The pilot had no formal instrument flying training or experience beyond that provided in his commercial helicopter flight training syllabus. 1.	The pilot was licensed and qualified for VFR flight.2.	The pilot did not hold an instrument rating nor was one required for the planned operation.3.	Records indicate that the helicopter was certified, equipped and maintained for the operation.4.	No indication was found of any pre-impact failure of the helicopter, its engine or systems. This report concludes the Transportation Safety Board's investigation into this occurrence. Consequently, the Board authorized the release of this report on 17 August 2000.

A98C0037: Upon engine start and taxi, the wing tip of a Points North Air Services DC-3 struck the wing tip of a parked Cessna Caravan.  The navagation light and lens on the DC-3 was broken and the wing tip on the Caravan was dented.The DC-3 had just been refuelled and during the refuelling process the Cessna Caravan parked on the ramp.  The DC-3 had a crew change and as the new captain began to taxi, he realized that there was not enough room to manoeuver by the Cessna Caravan.  The captain applied brakes, but could not prevent the wings tips from colliding.  The ramp was experiencing ongoing traffic congestion due to numerous air tankers hauling  fuel to northern communities.

A98A0127: A98A0127: Three Grumman TBM-3 water bombers departed Miramichi enroute to Woodstock to put on a water bombing demonstration.  Approximately 15 minutes into the flight C-GLEK experienced a complete engine failure.  (The pilot reported hearing two loud bangs followed by oil covering the windscreen and a complete power loss)  The pilot of the lead aircraft directed C-GLEK towards a clear cut area, however, because of large stumps in the clear cut, the pilot elected to over-fly the clear cut area and carry out a controlled crash into the trees rather than risk going end-over-end in the clear cut area.  The pilot was able to exit the aircraft by himself but was later taken to the hospital where he was held overnight for observations.The TSB will be attending an engine tear-down and will up-date the summary with the findings.

A99P0005:  The Air Canada A-340 (C-FYLU / ACA896) had just began the take-off roll on runway 08R at Vancouver International Airport, when at about 80 knots, the pilots received a warning light in the cockpit, indicating that a refuelling panel/door was open.  The pilots aborted the take-off below 100 knots; the pilot intentionally decelerated the aircraft slowly, using the all the remaining runway before vacating it at the far end at taxiway "D5".The pilots then stopped the aircraft on taxiway "D".  At that time, two airport fire trucks were returning along taxiway "D" to the fire hall after training exercises, and when they passed alongside the stationary aircraft, the fire crews saw smoke and flames coming from the right main landing gear.  Moments later, they saw flames from the left landing gear.They quickly approached that aircraft and commenced to spray the wheel assemblies with water; the fires were extinguished in seconds. The fire crew, however, were not able to communicate directly with the flight crew to inform them of the fire, but a Vancouver International Airport Authority supervisor arrived and began to speak to the pilots using the ground intercom system.  At the same time the flight crew were talking to their company and the Vancouver ground control, and were not aware of the fires, until the VIAA supervisor spoke to them.After a 15-minute monitoring period by ERS to ensure the gear assemblies were safe for the aircraft to continue moving, the aircraft was towed to the gate with the passengers on board.The aircraft was later towed to the company maintenance facility for inspection.  No fire damage or defect was found.  It is likely that the long roll-out after the RTO contributed to the brake overheat condition.  The operator reports that the refuelling panel/door had not been latched properly at the last refuelling.  More information to follow.

A99C0097: THE MANITOBA GOVERNMENT AIR SERVICES CANADAIR CL215 WATER BOMBER, C-GUMW, DEPARTED THUNDER BAY EN ROUTE TO ITS HOME BASE AT GIMLI, MB.  SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF, THE CREW FELT A SLIGHT VIBRATION, AND NOTED THAT THE BMEP (POWER OUTPUT) OF THE RIGHT ENGINE HAD DECLINED.  THE CREW DIVERTED THE FLIGHT BACK TO THUNDER BAY, WHERE THEY LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.  MAINTENANCE FOUND A CRACKED CYLINDER IN THE BACK ROW OF THE ENGINE.  THE CREW REPORTED THAT THE ENGINE HAD FUNCTIONED NORMALLY DURING THE PRE-TAKEOFF RUNUP.

A99P0070:   The Bell 206 Helicopter (C-FBQG) was manouvering above a steep hill side in support of a heli-logging operation, when the Chokers attached to the end of the external load Longline became snagged on a large log.  Witnesses reported that the helicopter reached extreme pitch attitudes before the Chokers released.  The Longline subsequently snagged another log.  The pilot appeared to lose control of the helicopter and experienced Dynamic Roll Over while attached to the ground by the Longline/external load. The Helicopter struck the ground, rolled over, and came to rest, held up by the Longline, on the hill side .  Ground crews reached the aircraft in time to temporarily put out a post-crash fire with the aircraft fire extinguisher, however a second fire ensued.  Without other appropriate fire fighting equipment, the ground crew were forced to quickly extricate the trapped pilot.  The fire consumed the aircraft, but was extinguished by a company helicopter (S61) which later transported the injured pilot to the Hope, B.C. hospital.  The pilot, who was wearing a helmet, received serious injuries to his right arm and torso.  His helmet displayed extensive impact damage and likely prevented serious head injuries. Preliminary information revealed no mechanical failure of the helicopter prior to impact.   NMH report:REPORT 99091A   07/27/99 		(Preliminary prepared 07/12/99)JUNE 18, 1999BELL 206B-IIC-FBQGHELI-LOGGING SUPPORTBOSTON BAR B.C. AREAComplete pilot records are available from the Flight Training department. Total time approximately 2,400 hours, total time on type - 500 hours, long line training (1998) - .6 hours, long line experience - 50 hours. At 17:10 on June 18, 1999 helicopter C-FBQG crashed while conducting support activities for a Sikorsky SK-61 Heli-logging operation near Boston Bar B.C. The crash site was at approximately 3000ASL, and the temp was 20C.  The exposure of the impact sight (slope) was westerly and while the winds were variable the interviews indicate they were upslope at about 20knots.  There were no passengers on board the helicopter at the time, the pilot sustained multiple injuries (serious) and the aircraft was destroyed in a post impact fire.At the time of the mishap the pilot was in the process of delivering bundles of chokers to the riggers on the hill.BACKGROUNDAlthough the pilot had been working in support of this particular heli-logging operation since May 30 1999, this was the first day that he was required to fly close support for the SK-61. Previously his activities involved crew set outs and pickups of both fallers and riggers, and limited longline delivery of choker bundles. On this particular day, the logging had shifted to a block that was much closer to the log delivery landing and therefore required a more continuous supply of choker delivery to the riggers. At the time of the mishap the SK-61 had just finished refueling at the service landing and was heading back up the hill, and the Bell 206 was delivering the last three bundles of chokers (for the day) to the riggers. There was one-half of a logging cycle (35 minutes) left to be completed that day.OCCURRENCEOf the three riggers working in the area of the accident, two had received their choker deliveries. The helicopter was bringing a bundle for the third rigger, and had two more hooked to the carousel for riggers on an adjacent block. As the helicopter arrived at the site the third rigger was getting a drink of water from his packsack. As he turned back he noticed the helicopter appeared to be sitting in a vertical hover, with the bundles resting on the ground, downslope from his ribbon stick (target for choker delivery). The helicopter was facing the slope as if the pilot was trying to locate the rigger or ribbon stick. A brief radio conversation occurred advising the pilot where the target was and the pilot acknowledged that he now had a visual confirmation. The rigger indicated during the post accident interview, that at that point the helicopter seemed to start nosing over and turning to the right as if the aircraft was going to move the choker bundles in that direction. As this movement began the aircraft rapidly pitched nose down and began a downward arc. It was later found that the bundles had not cleared the hill. The stringers used to attach the bundles to the carousel hooks had become caught between two large logs. See Investigation photographs included with this report.  As the aircraft continued in this downward arc it also rotated to the right 180 degrees (around the mast) until it was facing back up the longline, in a pronounced nose up, tail down attitude.The aircraft seemed to hang in this position, and was described as fluttering, wobbling, or waffling. After only a matter of seconds the aircraft seemed to launch over backwards, turning to the left while doing so, and impacted the slope in a nose down, left yawing manner. At this point the rigger who had virtually been looking thru the pilot's door, dove for cover as blades and other items began to be thrown in all directions.Investigation found that of the three carousel hooks being used at the time, one appears to have released, another was damaged and the stringer nubbin would have been released, and the third was actually ripped off of the carousel.When the noise of the impact subsided, the rigger radioed there was an aircraft down and he needed help. This call was the activation mechanism of the Heli-log Emergency Response Plan. He then ran downslope to the aircraft, which was resting on its left side, being held there by the longline, which was still attached to the helicopter (the carousel was caught in logs further upslope). See photographs.POST IMPACT The pilot was still restrained by the seatbelt and shoulder harness and did not appear to be conscious. The rigger began to check the pilot for a determination of injuries and was joined at that time by the other two riggers. At this point it was noted that there were flames visible around the turbine outlet area. One rigger directed the aircraft's Halon Fire Extinguisher at the flames while the second turned off the fuel valve itself. Due to the fact that the instrument panel had been torn back and to the right it is difficult to know whether this action had any effect. The three riggers began to administer first aid to the pilot who was starting to regain consciousness.A Supervisor, Maintenance Engineer, and another First Aid Attendant arrived at the site with the spine board and Level 3 First Aid Kit. It was noted that flames were again visible, not only from around the turbine area but also spreading to the hillside itself. The fire extinguisher was again directed at the flames but found to be exhausted and was of no further use. A decision was then made to immediately remove the pilot from the wreckage due to the increasing danger of fire and/or explosion. This was accomplished and the pilot was moved some 30 feet across the 60% slope where first aid was continued and attachment to the spine board carried out. Due to the increasing heat from the fire, a radio call went out for the SK-61 to bring it's Bambi Bucket and drop some water onto the fire.When the SK-61 arrived the injured pilot had been moved another 30 feet across slope and was being shielded from the fire and water by a large log and the crewmembers themselves. Two water drops were made which reduced the flame and heat substantially and the SK-61 returned to the service landing to reattach the longline and Emergency Stretcher Slinging Gear. Upon it's return the pilot and spine board were secured in the Ferno Stretcher and slung some 200 yards further up the hill to a landing where the ambulance and a number of vehicles were located. The First Aid attendants continued to stabilize the pilot for further transportation while the SK-61 returned to the service landing to drop the long line and install floorboards. Upon it's return, the injured pilot was then loaded internally into the SK-61 which then departed for the Fraser Canyon Hospital in Hope BC.  All persons involved in the emergency response, whether it be on the hill, in the SK-61, or back at the service landing did a commendable job under very adverse conditions and this cumulative action no doubt lead to the survival of the pilot. Only one and one-half hours had elapsed from the time of impact until the time of admittance to the Hospital in Hope. Due to complications involving internal injuries the pilot was transferred later that evening to the Chilliwack General Hospital where he underwent seven hours of surgery.Compound fractures to the right arm above and below the elbow were the most obvious injuries, however the rupture of the diaphragm combined with the resultant intrusion of various internal organs proved to be the most serious, and life threatening injury.

A99C0170: THE PILOT OF THE BELL 204B, C-GSHB, WAS ARRIVING AT A FIRE CAMP IN THE VICINITY OF CROSS LAKE, MB, TO PICK UP FIREFIGHTERS AT A NEWLY-CONSTRUCTED PAD.  THE PILOT MANEUVERED TO AVOID AN AREA CONTAINING PEOPLE, AND HAD DIFFICULTY IN MAINTAINING SIGHT OF THE PAD. JUST BEFORE TOUCHDOWN, THE TAIL ROTOR OF THE HELICOPTER STRUCK A TREE BRANCH, WHICH HAD NOT BEEN VISIBLE TO THE PILOT ON APPROACH TO THE SITE.  THE PILOT LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT, AND INSPECTED THE AIRCRAFT.  THE PILOT REPORTEDLY CONSIDERED THE AIRCRAFT SAFE FOR A FERRY FLIGHT AND FLEW THE AIRCRAFT TO NORWAY HOUSE WITH NO PASSENGERS.  ENGINEERS THERE FOUND DAMAGE TO THE TAIL ROTOR.  THEY REPLACED THE TAIL ROTOR, DRIVESHAFT AND ASSOCIATED GEAR BOXES IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE BELL REPAIR SCHEDULE.THE ACCIDENT WAS REPORTED ON 21 JULY 1999.  COMPANY OFFICIALS ADVISED THAT PERSONNELL INVOLVED WITH THE OCCURRENCE HAD BEEN INVOLVED WITH FIRE WORK IN THE FIELD AND HAD FOUND IT DIFFICULT TO REPORT THE OCCURRENCE AT AN EARLIER DATE.

A99C0208: THE SOWIND AIR PIPER PA-31-350, C-GHMK, WAS EN ROUTE FROM ST. ANDREWS, MB, TO BERENS RIVER.  ABOUT 40 NM SOUTH OF BERENS RIVER, THE PILOT NOTED A NOISE AND YAW FROM THE LEFT ENGINE. THE ENGINE LOST POWER, SMOKE WAS OBSERVED, AND THE COWLING WAS DISRUPTED.  THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO SECURE THE ENGINE, BUT WAS NOT ABLE TO FEATHER THE PROPELLER.  THE PILOT COMPLETED A FORCED LANDING ABOUT FIVE NM NORTH OF PRINCESS HARBOUR.  AFTER LANDING, THE NINE PASSENGERS AND ONE INFANT DEPARTED THE AIRCRAFT VIA THE EMERGENCY EXIT. THE PILOT ATTEMPTED TO EXTINGUISH THE FIRE IN THE LEFT ENGINE WITH THE HAND-HELD FIRE EXTINGUISHER, BUT WAS NOT SUCCESSFUL, AND THE FIRE CONSUMED THE AIRCRAFT FORWARD OF THE HORIZONTAL TAIL.  THE FIRE WAS SUBSEQUENTLY EXTINGUISHED BY A WATER BOMBER OPERATING IN THE AREA. EXAMINATION OF THE AIRCRAFT REVEALED THAT THE #2 CYLINDER OF THE LEFT ENGINE HAD DEPARTED THE ENGINE CASE.

A00C0178: The Jackson Air Services DeHavilland DHC-3 Otter was departing from an outpost camp at Stevens-Nicklin Lake, MB with a pilot and two camp employees and some camp equipment on board.  The camp was being evacuated because of the threat of a nearby forest fire. During initial climb, at about 80 feet agl, the aircraft began to descend, despite the application of full engine power, and settled into the trees.  The occupants were reportedly not injured by the crash, but sustained minor injuries exiting the aircraft.  The aircraft was destroyed by the impact with the trees and a post-crash fire.The local temperature was 27 degrees C, and the aircraft was near its maximum gross weight.  It was reported that the aircraft had a headwind in proximity to the forest fire on takeoff, and that it flew into the area of a tailwind during initial climb.

A00W0241: The Boeing 737-300, N17345, was on descent into Calgary when the forward cargo compartment fire warning light illuminated, and the fire warning bell sounded. The crew discharged the fire extinguishers, but the fire warnings continued. An emergency was declared, and an uneventful landing was completed with ERS in attendance. No evidence of fire was found, and the aircraft departed after the cargo fire suppression system was put on MEL and the fire bottles and parts replaced. Maintenance determined that the false warning was caused by a warning switch cannon plug that was not fully seated. It was secured and the system checked normal.

A00P0224: During climbout from Vancouver International, the crew of the Boeing 737 (C-GIPW) noted a momentary flash of the No. 1 fire handle. The aircraft had been dispatched with an unserviceable No.1 engine overheat and fire protection system (under the authority of MEL 26-02). As the climb continued above 10,000 feet, the flashing of the fire handle became imtermittent and the crew decided to return an to Vancouver. The crew requested ERS support and received a clearance to return. During the descent, the fire handle light illuminated steadily, as did the Master Caution light. The crew completed the primary fire precaution checklist and the No. 1 engine (P&W JT8D) was shut down. Following this activity, the crew completed the full fire checklist. The flight landed normally, with the fire trucks in attendance. The aircraft was brought to a full stop on the runway and, once the fire crews cleared it, they proceeded to the terminal and de-planed the passengers using the bridge. The passengers had been briefed about the situation during the descent, and again on the runway. The flight attendants were given a full de-brief.

A01W0180: The pilot of C-FKBM, an A26B water bomber executed a go-around while on approach to the Whitehorse airport (CYXY) due to an indication of unsafe gear position. The aircraft landed uneventfully  with AFF standing by as a precaution.  Company maintenance has determined the problem to be a faulty gear indicator micro switch.

A01W0176: The crew of the PBY-5, C-FNJE was conducting a water pick up from Sitidgi Lake during fire suppression activities when they lost control. A wing tip dug into the water and the aircraft came to rest nose down in the lake. Another PBY which was in the area landed on the lake near the downed machine and picked up the crew before it sank in about 100 feet of water.

A01A0092: WHILE ON CLIMB-OUT FROM HALIFAX FOR LBPIA, THE FLIGHT ATTENDANTS ON BOARD CMM 7164, A BOEING 737-200 (B732), REPORTED A BURNING SMELL IN THE CABIN. THE AIRCRAFT WAS APPROXIMATELY 7 MILES ON DEPARTURE FROM RWY 24 WHEN PILOT REQUESTED A RETURN TO LAND AT HALIFAX. A/C REQUESTED PRIORITY AND THE FIRE CREWS. TERMINAL VECTORED THE AIRCRAFT TO A LEFT DOWNWIND FOR RUNWAY 24.  AT APPROXIMATELY 3 MILES FINAL THE PILOT INFORMED TOWER THAT THE SMELL OF SMOKE WAS GONE. AFF ADVISED. AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AT 193OZ. UPDATE O8/O8/01THE RIGHT AIR CONDITIONING PACK TRIPPED OFF PRIOR TO ROTATION POSSIBLY DUE TO INGESTION OF A SMALL BIRD. MAINTENANCE WAS UNABLE TO DETERMINE IF THE PACK FAULT CAUSED THE BURNING ODOUR; HOWEVER THEY BELIEVE THAT IT IS LIKELY THAT BIRD INGESTION CAUSED THE BURNING SMELL AS FLIGHT ATTENDANTS LIKENED THE SMELL TO BURNING HAIR. THE ENGINES WERE INSPECTED AND THE AIRCRAFT WAS SUBSEQUENTLY RELEASED TO SERVICE.

A01W0198: During forest fire suppression activities, the pilot of CRC567, a Conair Fire Cat observed a low oil pressure light and dropping oil pressure on No. 2 engine. He shut down the engine (Wright 982 C9 HE2-MR5) and advised Whitehorse Intl (CYXY) control tower of his situation, requesting AFF response. The aircraft landed uneventfully at 1605 PST.  Inherent difficulties in ground handling of the Fire Cat with one engine inoperative, necessitated a tow off the airport manoeuvring area. Initial inspection of the engine revealed that a valve had failed.

A02W0098: The Bell 212, C-GRHA had conducted a sling load drop into a clearing during forest fire operations, and was hovering to allow a ground assistant to hook up the empty net, when the tail rotor contacted a tree. After four uncontrolled rotations to the right, the pilot put the aircraft on the ground with substantial damage to the tail boom and tail rotor drive train. There were no injuries to the pilot or the ground assistant who dove out of the way of the gyrating helicopter.

A02C0168: The Cypress Helicopters Ltd. Sikorsky S-58E, C-FFZM, was departing en route to a fire camp 25 nm nw of Big River, SK, on a cargo flight. During initial climb, the engine (Curtiss Wright R1820) backfired and momentarily lost power. It regained power, but backfired again and the pilot landed the aircraft in a marsh. The aircraft was consumed by a fuel-fed fire. The crew of two and the passenger evacuated the helicopter without injury and were evacuated from the marsh by another helicopter. The aircraft's engine had backfired 30 flight hours before the occurrence, and an inspection after that occurrence revealed a bent intake valve.

A03A0014: The Atlantic Coast Dornier 328, operating as BR6269, departed Runway 06 at Halifax for a scheduled flight to Boston. Two minutes after take-off the fire detection system indicatd a fire warning on the number one engine. The crew referenced the QRH and discharged both fire suppression bottles. The fire indication remained "on" and the crew declared an emergency. Crash alarm was activated and vehicles were in stand-by positions. The aircraft was vectored back to the airport where it landed safely on runway 24 at 07:16 AST. Maintenance inspected the number one engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada PW306B) and found no evidence of fire and they could not duplicate the fire indication. Maintenance replaced the fire control panel and one fire bottle for a ferry flight back to the Boston base.

A03C0133: The Provincial Helicopters Bell 204B, serial number 2043, registration C-FOKY had departed Norway House on a smoke patrol in support of forest fire fighting operations. The helicopter was established in cruise flight at 3000 ft (2200 ft agl) when, approximately 15 to 20 minutes into the flight, a banging noise was heard coming from the tail area followed by a slow and smooth 30 degree yaw to the left. The pilot gently applied opposite pedal and was able to correct the yaw. The banging was not repetitive, but appeared as pedal was applied. The pilot landed the helicopter straight ahead into a swampy area approximately 1/4 nm north of the Molsen Lake Lodge. The helicopter landed without incurring further damage or injury to the occupants.An examination of the helicopter revealed that one of the tail rotor pitch link bolts (AN 174-15 or subsequent) was missing and that the pitch link was hanging free from the tail rotor horn, but still attached on the opposite end to the crosshead assembly. One, or both of the tail rotors had struck the tail boom several times in flight causing the banging noise heard by the pilot and damage to the tail boom. The tail boom and tail rotor assembly is to be replaced in situ. More info to follow.Update:  The vertical stabilizer was struck several times by the disconnected blade only. An examination of the tail rotor blade grip horn pitch change bushings showed a wear lip on the outer circumference on the face of both bushings from movement or fretting with the pitch change link rod ends. The wear pattern was indicative of an under-torqued or loose bolt arrangement. Because of interference with the tail rotor trunnion spindle bearing caps, the pitch link change bolt would have to fail in order for the pitch change link to become disconnected in flight. As the bolt was not recovered, the mode of failure could not be determined. A TSB Occurrence Bulletin was issued.

A03A0076: The PZL M18 Dromader was number three of four aircraft conducting spray operations. The pilot reported engine (PLZ 1000) difficulties. Shortly after, the aircraft was seen to enter a spiral dive from less than five hundred feet and it did not recover. There was a post-impact fire, which initiated a forest fire. The pilot was fatally injured and the aircraft was destroyed.

A03P0220: NC AOR 31018: A Cessna 175 bearing the US registration N9238B had departed Salmon Arm for Keremeos with only the pilot on board. A landing was attempted in an unprepared field adjacent to a residential neighbourhood. Following touchdown, the pilot attempted to abort the landing and applied power. The aircraft lifted off and entered a steep climb to clear a row of trees at the end of the field. As it cleared the trees, the aircraft entered a steep left bank and crashed in the front yard of the house adjacent to the field. The aircraft severed the overhead electrical power line from the street to the house and came to rest straddling a fence in an upright position. The engine remained running as first responders attempted to extract the pilot. Fuel was leaking into the aircraft cabin and ignited, forcing rescuers to abandon their attempts. The local volunteer fire department arrived within minutes and extinguished the fire, however the pilot perished; there were no other injuries. Property damage was minimized by the action of the fire crews.

A03P0265:  The amphibious float-equipped deHavilland DHC-2 Beaver (C-GHAF) took off from Penticton airport at 1420 PDT and crashed in a box canyon about 10 nm north. A post impact fire broke out and consumed most of the cabin area. The 3 occupants were fatally injured.UPDATED: 15 OCTOBER 2004THE BOARD AUTHORIZED THE RELEASE OF THIS REPORT ON 07 SEPTEMBER 2004.SummaryThe amphibious, float-equipped de Havilland DHC?2 Mk. 1, Beaver, C?GHAF, serial number 1408, left Nanaimo, British Columbia, and landed at Penticton Airport at 1232 Pacific daylight time (PDT). The aircraft was fuelled with 184 litres of fuel, filling all three belly tanks. At this time, the rear portion of the aircraft cabin was observed to be loaded with luggage and cargo. The pilot/aircraft owner was planning his flight to Calgary (Springbank), Alberta, and spent at least an hour flight planning and talking with the Kamloops Flight Information Centre by telephone. He had some difficulty determining a route to fly to Springbank, because of airspace restrictions due to forest fires, but decided on a routing of Penticton, Kelowna, Vernon, Revelstoke, and Springbank.The aircraft took off from Penticton Airport at 1420 PDT, with the pilot and two passengers on board and crashed approximately seven minutes later in a ravine of Penticton Creek, 11 nautical miles northeast of Penticton Airport. A post-impact fire broke out and consumed most of the fuselage area. The fire caused a small forest fire, seen by a firefighting aircraft crew. There were no radio calls from the occurrence aircraft, and the three occupants were fatally injured.Findings as to Causes and Contributing Factors1.	As the aircraft approached high terrain in a climb, the pilot, for undetermined reasons, did not turn away from the terrain; the aircraft struck tree tops and crashed.2.	The aircraft's climb performance was adversely affected by density altitude and the relatively high aircraft weight, so that the aircraft was unable to clear the high terrain ahead.Findings as to Risk1.	The licenced passenger had not informed the TC medical examiner who conducted her last medical that she had been diagnosed with coronary artery disease, posing the risk that she could pilot an aircraft while not medically fit to do so.2.	The aircraft was being operated at a higher weight than was justified by the STC, under which it was converted to an amphibian. Some of the structural modifications called for by the STC for the higher weight had not been carried out.Other Findings1.	It could not be determined who was piloting the aircraft on the occurrence flight.
