A04W0071: The Abitibi Helicopters Ltd. Bell 205A-1 helicopter, registration C-GHUM, had departed the Springbank, AB airport for Bow River with a "Bambi Bucket" attached. Approximately 1 nm west of the airport, the bucket was seen to depart from the helicopter and land in a farm yard. The helicopter retrieved the bucket and returned to the airport. There was no damage to persons, animals or property. The company determined that the manual release system was misrigged. The system is to be re-rigged and test flown.

A04W0165: The Delta Helicopters Bell 206B, C-FDYO, was engaged in forest fire infra-red scanning. While manoeuvring at low level to return to a hot spot, the helicopter yawed uncontrollably to the right, completing a number of rotations before settling into small trees. The aircraft was substantially damaged. The pilot sustained serious soft tissue injuries to his back and the passenger received minor injuries. An ELT signal was received by RCC, and Alberta Forest Protection Service flight following reported the overdue helicopter. The occupants were unable to contact anyone on three different radios, however they were located approximately one hour later by another helicopter working on the same fire.Update 9 Sept:It was determined that the helicopter was flown in a tight "pedal turn" manoeuvre, and at the completion of the turn, the winds were at the right relative angle to induce a slight loss of tail rotor effectiveness. This was compounded by the immediate application of full left pedal and raising the collective, resulting in 4 - 5 rotations of the aircraft before settling into the trees.

A04O0233: The Skyservice Airlines Airbus A330-300 aircraft, registration C-FRAV, operating as flight SSV700, was enroute when the crew received a Master Warning for a lavatory smoke indication. The In-charge flight attendant reported there was an odour from the lavatory but no evidence of smoke or fire. The flight crew declared an emergency and returned to Toronto where ARFF was standing by for the uneventful landing. Once on the ground, an inspection was carried out by the fire crew but there was no indication of fire on the aircraft. The aircraft was then given clearance to taxi to the gate. Maintenance is continuing to investigate the cause of the smoke alarm in the lavatory, and the operator will report with further findings when they become available.

A05P0132: At 1532 Pacific daylight time on the 07 June 2005, a certification flight testing program was being conducted by Cascade Aerospace Inc. with a Bombardier DHC-8-402, serial number 4040,  modified for air tanker operations. The test flight curriculum included a series of increasing amplitude push-over/pull-up manoeuvres to evaluate stick-force-per-g (gravity) and to demonstrate satisfactory handling characteristics during a push-over to 0g with a water/retardant load on board. During the third and final push-over, the #1 and #2 engine low oil pressure annunciators both illuminated. The speed of both propellers then reduced by about 300 rpm and the engine torques increased proportionately (both events were uncommanded). A recovery to a normal attitude was completed during which both engine low oil pressure annunciators extinguished. The #1 propeller recovered back to the selected speed of 1020 rpm. However, the #2 propeller went into an overspeed condition and was governed at 1060 rpm by the overspeed governor. The #2 propeller was then intentionally feathered and the engine was shut down in accordance with the Aircraft Flight Manual checklist. The #2 engine was subsequently re-started, however, the propeller could not be un-feathered, so the engine was again shut down. The flight concluded at the departure point of Abbotsford with one engine inoperative.UPDATED: 15 JANUARY 2007THE BOARD AUTHORIZED THE RELEASE OF THIS REPORT ON 02 AUGUST 2006.

A05P0137: The aircraft had departed Abbotsford at 1853 Pacific daylight time, under VMC, for the sixth flight of the day, and proceeded to uncontrolled airspace about 15 nm north of Abbotsford. There were two pilots and two company flight test engineers on board. A certification flight testing program was being conducted by Cascade Aerospace Inc. with the Bombardier DHC-8-402, serial number 4040, modified for air tanker operations. At about 1930, during a rate one turn in cruise flight at 4 500 feet, the #1 engine (PW150A, serial number PCE-FA0020) shutdown without warning. The auto-feather system was dis-armed, in accordance with normal procedures and the alternate feather system was used to complete feathering of the propeller. The flight returned to Abbotsford at 1950 with one engine inoperative.  UPDATED: 15 JANUARY 2007THE BOARD AUTHORIZED THE RELEASE OF THIS REPORT ON 23 AUGUST 2006.

A05Q0211: The CL-600-2B19 (RJ), registered C-GMJA operated by Air Canada Jazz was parked at the gate when ramp crew noticed an APU fire. Flight crew also received fire indications in the flight deck and airport fire crew was called. Passengers were deplaned by the main cabin door. The fire was extinguished without further incident.Report from the maintenance indicated that the fire was contained in the APU (Garrett GTCP 36-150) and some components where found seized. The APU was replaced and the aircraft returned to service.

A05W0250: The Slave Air (1988) Ltd. Beech King Air B200, C-FSAT, was departing from runway 25 at the Valley View, AB airport approximately one hour before sunrise. During the final stages of the take off roll, the pilot flying noticed a large brown object off to one side followed by a thud. The flight crew rejected the take-off and the aircraft was brought to a stop with 20 feet of runway remaining. The remains of a medium sized deer were found on the runway. Damage from the impact required repairs to the left main gear doors and left propeller and the removal of the left engine for a hot section overhaul. Update 23 January 2006: TC Aerodrome Safety reported that the Vallyview airport is a registered aerodrome rather than a certified site and therefore is not required to have a bird and wildlife program. In light of the oil boom and the communities geographic local the town about six months ago commissioned at feasibility study to look at the cost/ benefit of lengthening the existing runway from 3300 -5000 feet and have the aerodrome certified. An upgrade of this magnitude would allow air tanker aircraft CL 215, Fire Cat's and Convair 580's to operate out of Vallyview and offer the town a scheduled air service.This deer strike was the first time an event such as this as ever occurred since the inception of the airport there. The town does provide runway condition reports to incoming charter flights, and maintains the runway and apron lighting as well as their surfaces.

A07Q0111: The Bell 206B, registration C-GSHC, was assigned to the mapping of a forest fire 22 nm south-west of Chibougamau.  The aircraft was flown approximately 150 ft AGL, at low airspeed, in high winds reported at 11 kts gusting 18 kts. While upwind, the pilot backed up slightly to give a better view of the fire perimeter to the two passengers doing mapping. The aircraft lost tail rotor effectiveness, did several 360 degree turns before descending into the trees and severing the tailboom. A post-impact fire started but was quickly extinguished by the pilot who had already exited the aircraft. He closed the fuel valve, all electrical systems and used the fire extinguisher.  The pilot confirmed that the ELT was ON. When no position report was given to the fire dispatch at the appropriate time, a helicopter was sent to look for them. They were evacuated to the local hospital. The passengers sustained minor injuries . The pilot was not hurt.  The aircraft was destroyed.

A07P0357: At 1602 Pacific daylight time, the privately registered Piper PA-34-200 Seneca (registration C GHFD, serial number 34-7350210) was cleared for takeoff from Runway 08 Right at the Vancouver International Airport destined for Pitt Meadows Regional Airport. The flight was operating under visual flight rules with only the pilot on board. Shortly after takeoff, communications and radar contact were lost. The aircraft collided with a 15-storey residential building in Richmond, about 1.5 nautical miles east-southeast of the departure end of Runway 08 Right. The pilot was fatally injured. There was no post-impact fire. The aircraft entered a suite occupied by two people; one received serious non-life-threatening injuries, the other received minor injuries. Structural damage to the building was minimal, but there was extensive water damage from the fire suppression system. As a result, hundreds of people were displaced from their homes for extended periods. There were no other reported injuries. UPDATE: 23 SEPTEMBER 2009THE BOARD AUTHORIZED THE RELEASE OF THIS REPORT ON 20 AUGUST 2009.

A08W0023: The First Air Aerospatiale ATR42-300, C-FIQR was parked at the Yellowknife Braden-Burry Expediting ramp after a flight from Ekati mine, NT (CYOA). While the passengers were deplaning, the right engine (P&W 120) was running with the propeller brake engaged (H Mode). As the crew was shutting down the engine, they received a "Prop Unlock" warning light, and flames were noticed emitting from the engine. The "On Ground Engine Fire" checklist was actioned, including discharging the fire bottles. An emergency was declared on ground frequency. ARFF responded, but their services were not required, since the fire had been extinguished by the aircraft fire suppression system. There were no reported injuries or damage to the aircraft beyond that sustained by the propeller brake.

A08C0166: The Boeing 747-400 freighter, operated by Cathay Pacific Airways as flight CPA092, was cruising en route when the crew received a forward cargo fire warning indication. The crew carried out emergency procedures which included activating on board fire suppression systems, declared an emergency, and diverted the flight to Winnipeg. During the diversion the fire warning terminated and the flight landed on runway 18 without further incident. After landing, the aircraft was stopped on runway 13 for inspection by ARFF staff who determined the fire warning had been false.

A08Q0186: The Airbus A320, registration C-FMSX, was on the initial climb out of CYUL Montreal Pierre Elliott Trudeau Int'l for CYYZ Toronto LBP Int'l when the crew received a fire warning in the aft hold. The fire bottles were discharged, an emergency was declared and the aircraft returned to land CYUL. Runway 06L/24R was closed for a period of 15 minutes while fire crews checked for heat and fire; no signs of smoke or fire were found. Smoke detectors (SDCU), fire bottles and squibs were replaced as per the maintenance manuals. Aircraft returned to service.

A09P0007:  The Air Canada regional (Jazz) CRJ aircraft, C-FDJA, operating as JZA460, took off from Vancouver for Fort McMurray.  During the climb, about 90 nm north of Vancouver the crew received a cargo smoke warning, followed shortly after by a cargo fan fail message.  The crew completed the QRH checklist, discharged the cargo fire suppression bottles, declared an emergency, and returned to Vancouver, where the aircraft landed on runway 26R without further difficulty, with ARFF on standby.  The cargo smoke warning persisted for about 5 minutes after activation.

A09Q0075: The Quebec Government CL215 water bomber, registration C-FTXK, was 10 nm northwest of the CYQB VOR at 5000 ft on a training flight when the right engine (Pratt & Whitney PW 2800) backfired three times. After checking the engine parameters and adjusting the mixture to full rich, the engine ran smoothly. The flight was continued until the right engine backfired again while executing low speed manoeuvres and simulated engine failures in cruise flight. The crew elected to shut the engine down and feather the propeller. All checks were executed and the crew requested the presence of emergency vehicles. The aircraft landed normally at CYQB and taxied under its own power to the company hangar. A maintenance inspection revealed a problem with the ignition system. The engine was repaired and returned to service.

A10W0105: The Ultra Helicopters Ltd. AS350BA helicopter, C-FXMJ, landed in a clearing about 50 nm north of Wabasca, AB to pick up a fire crew. After liftoff and acceleration through 30 knots, a main rotor vibration was detected, and the aircraft was landed in a clearing about 800 meters away. Two main rotor blades had sustained substantial damage in the trim tab area, likely from contact with a tree. The helicopter was grounded on-site, and due to fading daylight, the pilot and four passengers were extracted the next day.

A11P0028: Shortly after take off from Runway 13 at Courtenay Airpark, at about 50 feet altitude, the amateur-built Van's RV-4 engine (Lyc. O-320D2A) stopped. The pilot headed straight ahead and landed hard along the shoreline. The main landing gear was damaged, and the propeller struck the ground.  The tide was low at the time and the aircraft was out of the water. The RCMP and fire crews responded. The aircraft was moved to keep it out of the water at high tide. The pilot observed some white crystalline substance in suspension when he dipped the tanks during an earlier stop at Port Alberni, and noted a relatively dark blue tint to the fuel from that location.The engine and fuel system will be examined further to assess any possible fuel blockage or contamination.

A11A0027: The Lufthansa Airbus A340-311, registration D-AIGB, was operating as DLH420 on a flight from Frankfurt, Germany to Boston, MA when the flight crew received the ECAM message "SMOKE CAB REST SMOKE"; indication of possible fire in the aircraft's mobile crew rest area (MCR). Since the area was occupied, the flight crew established communication with the rest crew to confirm that the fire warning was not accidentally triggered. No smoke or fire was observed but one of the rest crew thought a smell could be detected briefly.  The MCR was evacuated and the flight crew activated the fire extinguishing system, declared an emergency, and obtained a clearance to descend to FL250 and divert to the nearest airport, Goose Bay, NL. The cabin was prepared for an emergency landing and passengers were re-briefed on evacuation procedures. The flight continued to Goose bay and landed without incident with ARFF standing by.The aircraft was shutdown to allow fire crew to inspect the MCR and when no sign of heat or combustion could be detected, the aircraft was restarted and taxied to ramp where passengers deplaned normally. Maintenance personnel inspected the MCR and adjacent cargo compartment and passenger cabin areas for evidence of heat or combustion without any sign being detected.  A smoke detection control unit inspection was performed without fault and the system was reset.  The MCR was blocked according to MEL for the return flight to Frankfurt. The flight back to Frankfurt was without any problem.Further trouble shooting was performed after arrival in Frankfurt in conjunction with a detailed action order without fault and the aircraft was returned to service.

A11W0126: The Mustang Helicopters Eurocopter AS350-B2, C-FMNE, had departed Livingston Gap Fire Base in Alberta and was approximately 5 miles out when the pilot was alerted by a hydraulic warning light and horn. The hydraulic system was shut off as per the flight manual and the flight returned to the base. Upon coming into a low hover, control was lost and the main rotor blades struck the ground. An upright but hard landing resulted. It was reported that the pilot received a serious injury, and of the 4 passengers on board, one received a minor injury. The operator will report back to the TSB when on scene, and the TSB will follow up with hydraulic system component tests.Update 29 August: The pilot was not injured. Site survey confirmed that the impending bypass indication had popped out on the hydraulic system. The TSB will investigate further.Update 24 Oct: All 3 servos were tested at the Eurocopter Canada facilities under the supervision of a TSB investigator. In addition the hydraulic pump and belt, pressure sending unit, tank and wiring harness were inspected. Other than expected bendingwith the resultant binding from the impact, all servos operated within normal parameters. The other components had no anomalies.

A11A0085: The Provincial Airlines Ltd. Saab 340A aircraft (registration C-FPAI) was operating as SPR908 on a flight from St. Anthony, NL (CYAY) to St. John's, NL (CYYT). While en-route to CYYT, a burning smell was noticed. The crew shut off the recirculation fans and consulted the QRH checklist after which the smell seemed to dissipate. When the smell was again noted, the crew elected to divert to Gander, NL (CYQX) and declared an emergency shortly thereafter. The burning smell dissipated once more and the flight landed without incident at CYQX with ARFF crews standing by. Fire crews confirmed that no indication of fire was present and followed the aircraft as it taxied to the terminal where the passengers deplaned normally. Company maintenance inspected the aircraft, replaced the right air cycle machine (ACM) for a suspected bearing failure and returned the aircraft to service.

A13O0038: Jazz flight JZA7945, a Canadair CL-600-2B19 (C-GJZZ) aircraft, was departing Toronto LBPIA when the flight crew received a lavatory smoke indication along with reports of an electrical burning smell in the cabin. No smoke was visible in the cabin or cockpit. An emergency was declared, the aircraft returned to Toronto and landed without further incident. The aircraft was stopped on a taxiway and inspected by fire crews using IR cameras. No signs if fire or hotspots were detected. The aircraft was cleared to the gate. Maintenance found two burn marks on the back of a light assembly.

A13P0028: At 14:24 PDT (21:24 Z) the Boeing 767-300, JA653J, operated by Japan Airlines as flight JAL17, was planning to depart Vancouver for Narita, Japan (RJAA) when the takeoff from Runway 26L was aborted. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop just west of Runway 12. ARFF was advised. JAL17 exited Runway 26L onto Lima 2 and then held on taxiway Lima and fire crews inspected the brakes. JAL17 was escorted to the deicing bay and water was applied to cool the brakes. All eight main tires deflated. The crew advised ATS that the aborted takeoff was due to a possible bird strike and injestion on the left engine. Fire crews reported possible fan blade damage on left engine. Runway 26L was inspected for debris but nothing was found.

A14W0003: The First Air ATR 42-300 (C-FIQU) operating as flight FAB120 from Yellowknife, NT (CYZF) to Hay River, NT (CYHY) was taxiing for departure when the flight attendant noticed smoke and notified the flight crew. The aircraft was taxied back to the ramp and a request for ARFF was made. The crew completed smoke / electrical smoke checklist followed by ramp shutdown checklist. The aircraft was met by fire crew and company maintenance. Smoke had subsided to allow for a normal deplaning of passengers and crew. The source of smoke was identified as a speaker transformer located on left bin #4 which was found burnt and electrically shorted. The transformer has been replaced and an SDR to Transport Canada was submitted.

A14P0011: A DeHavilland DHC-8-311, C-FACV, operated by Jazz from Vancouver to Penticton as Flight JZA8350 was waiting on taxiway 'Lima' to depart runway 08R when a flight attendant noticed the No 1 (left) engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada PW123, SN PCE123062) was smoking. The flight crew were advised, shutdown both engines, and discharged the fire suppression agent into the left engine compartment. They passed the information to ATC and ARFF responded; they confirmed there was no further indication of fire. The aircraft was towed back to the gate and passengers were off-loaded there.

A14W0131: The United States registered Piper PA-14, N4279H, was on a flight from Red Deer, AB to Grande Prairie, AB with a final destination in Alaska. The flight encountered heavy smoke from forest fires and slowed up due to poor visibility. Near Grande Prairie the pilot reported running out of fuel and was heading for a road for a forced landing. The flight ended on an unoccupied baseball diamond. There was substantial damage to the aircraft; no injuries to the 2 occupants and no post-crash fire.

A14W0141: The Federal Express Boeing 777F28 Freighter, N880FD, was operating as flight FDX195 from Memphis, TN (KMEM) to Anchorage, AK (PANC). En route to PANC, the flight crew received a cabin fire indication. The flight crew declared an emergency with ATC and diverted to Whitehorse, YT (CYXY). FDX195 landed uneventfully with ARFF standing by. ARFF crews inspected the aircraft and determined no fire present. Update 23 September 2014: Main deck fire suppression penetrator module (part number VAFSS7500-501) at position 2R replaced.

N114HQ, an Embraer 170-200LR aircraft operated by Republic Airlines, was conducting flight RPA4496 from Toronto/Lester B. Pearson Intl, ON (CYYZ) to Philadelphia Intl, PA (KPHL). During the climb after takeoff from CYYZ, the flight crew declared an emergency due to the forward cargo compartment fire suppression system failure. The aircraft returned to CYYZ and landed uneventfully with ARFF standing by. The operator’s maintenance placed the FWD Cargo Fire EXT on MEL 26-23-00-1 and eventually replaced the forward compartment fire bottle. An operational check was performed and no further faults were found. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-FDZT, a privately operated Cessna 180J aircraft, was conducting a VFR flight from High Level, AB (CYOJ) to Edmonton/Villeneuve, AB (CZVL). During cruise flight, the pilot experienced reduced visibility from forest fire smoke and elected to divert to Slave Lake, AB (CYZH). The pilot conducted an approach to Runway 10, however flared too high and the aircraft descended at a high rate toward the runway. The aircraft landed hard, bounced and subsequently settled down with the right wing tip and right horizontal stabilizer contacting the runway surface. The aircraft continued the landing roll and exited the runway with no further issues. The pilot, sole occupant, was uninjured. The ELT was not activated.

C-GENM, a Bombardier DHC-8-402 aircraft operated by WestJet Encore was conducting flight WEN3205 from Fort St. John, BC (CYXJ) to Vancouver Intl., BC (CYVR) with 4 crew members and 44 passengers on board. After departing CYXJ enroute to Vancouver, the #2 engine fire warning illluminiated. The flight crew shut down the engine and activated the fire suppression system. Both extinguisher bottles were discharged, however the #2 engine fire warning persisted. The flight crew advised air traffic control, declared an emergency and diverted to Prince George, BC (CYXS). The aircraft landed uneventfully at with airport rescue and fire fighting (ARFF) crews standing by. The operator’s maintenance established that there had not been an engine fire. The warning had been the result of a damaged wire in a connector within the fire detection system. The system was repaired and the aircraft returned to service.

C-FPPN, an Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 aircraft operated by Dam Helicopters, was conducting fire suppression activities approximately 17 nm Southeast of Trail, BC (CAD4). During the landing phase, while dropping off an initial crew, the pilot heard a loud buzzing noise and felt a vibration in the tail rotor system. The pilot landed and shut down the aircraft. A visual inspection of the tail rotor system did not find any abnormalities. After consultation with maintenance personnel, the pilot completed a ground run, flight test and then flew the aircraft back to Castlegar, BC (CYCG). Further inspection of the tail rotor revealed that contact with an unknown object had occurred. The tail rotor blade assembly was replaced in accordance with the manufacturer.

C-GHXO, a Cessna 180J aircraft operated by Trek Aerial Surveys, was conducting pipeline patrols approximately 30 nm East of Fort St. John, BC (CYXJ) with one pilot and one observer on board. The area of inspection features a significant amount of oil and gas production infrastructure. After flying for about 3 hours, the amount of forest fire smoke had increased significantly. Coincidentally, the pilot and the observer began to feel out of sorts; cognition was reduced. The pilot decided to head back to CYXJ out of precaution and while en route, the ability to concentrate became more difficult for both the pilot and the observer. ARFF was on standby for the landing, which was uneventful. Both the pilot and observer were met by EMS for observation and nothing significant was noted. The aircraft exhaust system was checked for leaks, and none were found.

C-GWCY, a Boeing 737-600 aircraft operated by WestJet, was conducting flight WJA137 from Calgary Intl (CYYC), AB to Vancouver Intl (CYVR), BC with 5 crew members and 99 passengers on board. Approximately 5 minutes prior to the top of descent, the lead flight attendant informed the pilots that a sulphur like smell was observed in the overhead bins, in the vicinity of Row 2. The flight crew declared a PAN PAN, and landed without further incident. Once at the gate, a fire crew proceeded on board and identified a smell from a WestJet commissary cooler bag in the overhead bin, above Row 2. The bag was removed and searched with no heat source identified. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-FBRP, a Cessna 525B aircraft operated by Tricycle Lane Aviation, was conducting a private flight from Scottsdale (KSDL), AZ to Calgary Intl (CYYC), AB with 2 pilots and 4 passengers on board. During the turn to final approach at CYYC at approximately 2000 feet AGL, the flight crew received a BAGGAGE SMOKE indication. The flight crew carried on with the approach, and declared an emergency. The aircraft landed without incident, vacated the runway, and was met by ARFF. No smoke was present; the flight crew elected not to evacuate the aircraft. Fire crews inspected the aircraft and no heat source was detected. The operator’s maintenance inspected the forward and aft baggage compartment smoke detection system. No faults were found. The issue was entered into the operator’s Safety Management System (SMS) for tracking, and the aircraft was released back to service.

On 04 May 2019, the Lakes District Air Service Ltd. Cessna 182E (registration C-FLVN, serial number 18253755) was conducting a fire surveillance flight under daytime visual flight rules. The flight was being conducted on behalf of the BC Wildfire Service in the vicinity of Smithers, British Columbia, with the pilot and 3 crew members on board. Approximately 3 hours into the flight, the pilot transmitted a Mayday before communication was lost. The 406 MHz emergency locator transmitter activated on impact and its signal was received by the Canadian Mission Control Centre. A helicopter search was conducted and the aircraft wreckage was located in a forested area approximately 50 nautical miles north of Smithers, 500 feet north of the Babine River, 5.6 nautical miles east of the Silver Hilton Lodge airstrip. The aircraft had collided with trees and terrain. One crew member survived the crash and was transported to hospital by helicopter. The pilot and the other 2 crew members were fatally injured. The aircraft was destroyed; there was no post-impact fire.UPDATED: 26 MAY 2020

C-FYDN, a privately registered Piper PA-12 aircraft on floats, was conducting a flight from an outpost camp at Domain Lake, ON to another outpost camp at Optic Lake, ON with 1 pilot and 1 passenger on board. The aircraft was reported overdue at destination, and was found near the shore of Domain Lake the following day by another aircraft. C-FYDN collided with terrain, and the accident caused a forest fire. The Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources responded to the forest fire, and the Ontario Provincial Police subsequently attended to the scene. The 2 occupants were fatally injured, and the aircraft was destroyed. No ELT signal was detected.

C-GKGA, a Beech 1900C operated by Skylink Express Inc. as flight SLQ720, was enroute from Winnipeg/James Armstrong Richardson INTL (CYWG), MB to Regina INTL (CYQR), SK with a crew of 2 onboard. During descent into CYQR, the crew heard a thump followed by a split in engine RPM and a slight yaw movement of the aircraft. Efforts to correct the split in engine RPM revealed the right propeller lever was jammed. The crew noticed the right engine (PT6A-65B) cowling had dislodged and remained only partially in place. The crew declared a PAN PAN with CYWG center and continued on to CYQR. The aircraft landed safely and came to a stop on the runway where they were met by fire crew for inspection. The aircraft then taxied off the runway. An inspection of the aircraft confirmed the right upper engine cowl had dislodged and interfered with the propeller governor, jamming the propeller control arm.

N806NW, an Airbus A330-323 aircraft operated by Delta Air Lines, was conducting flight DAL30 from Hartsfield/Jackson Atlanta (KATL), GA to London/Heathrow (EGLL), England. When in cruise flight at about 233 nm east-southeast of St. John’s (CYYT), NL, the flight crew smelled a wood smoke odour in the cockpit. The flight crew contacted cabin crewmembers, who confirmed smelling the odour in the cabin as well. The flight crew subsequently declared an emergency, began descending and completed the quick reference handbook (QRH) procedure for smoke and fumes; however, the odour did not dissipate. Following a discussion with company maintenance personnel, the flight crew decided to divert to CYYT where the flight landed without further incident. Maintenance personnel inspected the cabin, cargo, and avionics compartments and reported no finding of smoke or haze. No faults were recorded by aircraft systems. On 22 October 2020, multiple flights across eastern Canada reported the detection of smell related to smoke carried aloft at high altitude in Canadian airspace, which originated from ongoing wildfires in Colorado.

The Sky Regional Airlines Embraer 175 (AC7505, C-FXJC) was parked at the gate in Ottawa/ MCIA (CYOW)and was boarding for the flight to Toronto/ LBPIA (CYYZ). Approximately half of the passengers were boarded when the flight crew heard "FIRE" from the cabin and noticed smoke coming from the heater attached to the bridge. Boarding was stopped, and the ground crew began to use fire extinguishers on the heater; ARFF also responded to the scene. The captain decided not to deplane the passengers due to the location of the faulty heater underneath the bridge, but had passengers deplane after it was safe to do so. The aircraft was covered on the left side with the retardant residue, and after company maintenance was contacted it was decided to remove aircraft from service until a thorough inspection of the aircraft was completed. No damage was found and after cleaning the aircraft it was returned to service.

C-FGPC, a privately registered Cessna 185F on amphibious floats, departed Prince George International Airport (CYXS), BC  to Mackenzie (CYZY), BC  with 2 persons on board. The flight was occurring under special VFR with forest fire smoke in the area limiting the visibility to 2 1/4 sm. Upon departure, the visibility deteriorated as the aircraft climbed. CYXS ATC asked the pilot to deviate their heading to accommodate inbound traffic. The deviation placed the aircraft in an area with even less visibility so the pilot elected to descend and follow the Fraser River northbound. As the river became more difficult to follow, the pilot elected to land on it. The landing gear had not been retracted after take off and upon touchdown the aircraft flipped over. Both occupants managed to egress the overturned aircraft and climb onto one of the floats while waiting for rescue. The pilot received minor injuries and the passenger received serious injuries. The aircraft was substantially damaged.

C-GGFP, a Jazz Aviation LP. De Havilland DHC-8-402, operating as flight JZA416, was en route from Vancouver Int'l (CYVR), BC, to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 4 crew members and 38 passengers on board. The initial approach, approximately 23 nautical miles North of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. During this approach, the flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent through 10000 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to CYVR and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. Subsequent to the flight, maintenance actions included a severe turbulence inspection with no faults being found. The aircraft was returned to service.See occurrences A21P0085 and A21P0087 in relation to the same turbulence event.

C-FCMR, a Central Mountain Air Beech (Textron) 1900D was operating as flight GLR728 from Prince George (CYXS), BC to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 2 crew members and 12 passengers on board. The initial approach, approximately 24 nautical miles North of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. The flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent between 12000 feet and 11000 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to Penticton (CYYF), BC, and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. See occurrences A21P0085 and A21P0086 in relation to the same turbulence event

C-FQWE, a WestJet Encore De Havilland DHC-8-402, operating as flight WEN3324, en route from Vancouver Int'l (CYVR), BC, to Kelowna (CYLW), BC, with 4 crew members and 46 passengers on board. The flight's initial approach, approximately 24 nautical miles north of CYLW, was in the vicinity of the White Rock Lake forest fire. During the approach, the flight experienced severe turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions while in descent through 9500 feet above sea level. The flight crew discontinued the approach. The flight diverted to CYVR and landed without further incident. There were no injuries. Subsequent maintenance actions included a severe turbulence inspection; no faults were found. The aircraft was returned to service.See occurrences A21P0086 and A21P0087 in relation to the same turbulence event

C-FRJA, a Bombardier CL-600-2D24 (Series 900) aircraft, operated by Jazz Aviation LP (JZA7461), departed Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport (CYYZ) ON, destined for Chicago O’Hare International Airport, Chicago (KORD). After leveling off at FL380 the flight crew observed a flap caution message. They actioned the appropriate QRH checklist, contacted maintenance and decided to return to YYZ. The flight crew declared a PAN PAN in order to ensure they would get runway 23 for a long final approach, and requested emergency equipment on standby. The aircraft landed without further incident. After exiting the runway, fire crews inspected the brakes and tires with no damage or heat concerns noted.

C-FDOD, a Bell 412 helicopter operated by Wisk-Air Ltd., was returning 4 drums containing Jet A-1 (UN 1863) fuel from a cache near Prospect Lake, ON to the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (OMNR) fire base at Red Lake, ON. The pilot supervised the loading and the sling gear had been inspected and found serviceable prior to departure. After takeoff the pilot de-activated the electrical release on the cyclic control. Approximately 8 minutes later the load of 4 fuel drums fell to the ground. All of the drums were damaged and 3 released their contents. The remaining drum still held fuel. The fuel drums were retrieved by OMNR personnel on 12 June and remediation of the site was conducted. Details of the event were reported to CANUTEC. The operator reported that abrasion to the retaining strap connecting the load to the belly hook indicated that it had worked itself around and under the hook keeper. The hook and release mechanism were inspected and found serviceable. The emergency foot release had not been used. The operator's aircrews that used the same helicopter type and hook system were notified.

C-FTHY, a Talon Helicopters Limited Airbus AS350-B2 (A-Star) helicopter, was conducting external load operations 46 NM NW of Vernon (CYVK), BC, in support of forest fire suppression operations with 1 pilot on board. During cruise, the empty net which was attached to the long line, inadvertently released onto a steep hillside within the fire area. There were no injuries.The hook was inspected and the keeper was found to be sticky. The keeper was lubricated and function tested. Ground crews received additional briefings on sling operations.

C-GNTM, an Air Tractor AT-802 operated by Forest Protection Limited, was conducting fire suppression training flights about 20 nm southwest of Fredericton (CYFC), NB. It was planned to have the aircraft land at Brockway (CCX3) Airport, NB for fuel, and as the aircraft touched down on Runway 22 at CCX3, the aircraft began to drift to the left. The pilot applied right rudder, and when the yaw to the left continued, the pilot began adding right brake pedal pressure in an attempt to arrest the left yaw. It was not possible for the pilot to arrest the left yaw with right rudder and brake pedal force, and the left yaw increased until the aircraft nose was 90 degrees left, relative to the runway. The tailwheel pylon separated during the skid to the left, and the aircraft came to rest with the main landing gear off of the runway surface. The pilot was uninjured. The left mainwheel tire was found deflated due to a shredded patch in the center of the tread. The tire came off its wheel bead, and allowed the wheel rim to cause minor gouging damage to the chip seal runway surface. A small amount of fuel vented onto the runway surface. The landing conditions for runway were described as a light, right crosswind.

N744CK, a cargo-configured Boeing 747-400 operated by Kalitta Air, was conducting flight CKS636 from Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky Intl (KCVG), USA to Anchorage/Ted Stevens Intl (PANC), USA. While enroute, the flight crew received multiple status messages for Cargo FWD 1 and 2, fire Protection loops A and B.  Subsequently, the EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) displayed FIRE CARGO FWD warning message, as well as a Master Warning message, and the audible fire bell. The crew completed the cargo fire procedures and discharged the fire suppression system into the forward cargo compartment.  The crew then declared an emergency with Winnipeg Center and initially turned toward Cold Lake/Group Captain R.W. McNair (CYOD), AB when the aircraft was approximately 25 NM south-southwest of Flin Flon, MB. Winnipeg Center suggested to the crew that Saskatoon/John G. Diefenbaker Intl (CYXE) was closer, and the crew agreed that was a better option.  The crew proceeded towards CYXE and jettisoned fuel in order to decrease the aircraft weight to the maximum landing weight.  The aircraft landed safely at CYXE. Airport Emergency Services then approached the aircraft and scanned for heat sources with a thermal detector. No heat sources were detected, and the crew and Airport Emergency Services agreed it was safe to taxi the aircraft to a parking area. Once the crew was safely off the aircraft, the forward cargo compartment was opened. The discharge of the fire suppression was confirmed, and no damage to aircraft was noticed. The operator’s maintenance later determined that the fire indication was due to a fault in the fire detection system as they found evidence of AFOLTS cards shorted due to water damage. The cards were replaced, a thorough check of the system was carried out, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FGKJ, a cargo-configured Boeing 757-200 operated by CargoJet Airways Ltd., departed Winnipeg/James Armstrong Richardson Intl (CYWG), MB with a destination of Montreal/Mirabel Intl (CYMX), QC. Approximately 45 minutes after takeoff, the crew was alerted to a fire indication on the left engine (Rolls-Royce RB211-535E4-37). The crew carried out an in-flight shutdown of the left engine, declared an emergency, and, upon consulting company operations, elected to return to CYWG. The crew did not deploy the fire suppression system as the fire indication cleared when the engine was idled down during the shutdown procedure. The aircraft landed without further issues. The operator’s maintenance inspected the aircraft and a defect in the fire detection system is suspected. Troubleshooting and maintenance is being performed with company and engine manufacturer resources.

C-FRTW, an Air Canada Boeing 787-9 (Dreamliner) was conducting flight AC64 from Incheon International (RKSI), Seoul, Republic of Korea, to Vancouver International (CYVR), BC, with 12 crew and 300 passengers on board. After landing in CYVR, with the aircraft at the gate and the passengers deplaning, the ground crew noticed the left main gear showing smoke with a small fire present. The crew was advised and a rapid deplanement was conducted for the remaining passengers. An aircraft rescue and firefighting crew attended the scene to monitor the situation. No retardant was used, and the smoke and fire extinguished on its own.Maintenance conducted an inspection and replaced the No. 5 wheel assembly and the No. 5 brake assembly. Both assemblies that were removed have been sent for further inspection.

C-FFQV, a Conair Group Incorporated De Havilland Aircraft of Canada DHC-8-402AT air tanker, departed Abbotsford (CYXX), BC, as flight FGD547, to conduct firebombing training in the vicinity of Harrison Lake, BC with 2 crew members on board. After the fourth drop, the crew were alerted that the retardant tank doors did not close. The associated warning alarm could not be silenced and interfered with crew communication with air traffic control. The flight returned to the CYXX area and, after discussions with ground-based maintenance, the crew reset the retardant tank system which eventually silenced the tank door warning. When the crew lowered the landing gear, the gear warning horn became active and could not be silenced. The crew declared a "PAN PAN" emergency and conducted a low pass for a visual inspection by CYXX Tower controller. The controller confirmed the aircraft appeared normal and the crew landed without further incident.Maintenance personnel were unable to replicate the fault on the ground and a subsequent flight was conducted with no faults found. Maintenance and engineering have developed supplementary quick reference handbook procedures for resetting the tank door system and audio alerts. They are developing dedicated reset switches for the door and audio alert systems.

C-GRUV, a Valhalla Helicopters Inc. Bell 205A-1, was operating in support of forest fire fighting activities in the vicinity of Haig Lake, AB, 55 nm NE of Peace River Airport (CYPE), AB. Shortly after departure to commence bucketing operations the helicopter collided with terrain. The pilot, who was the sole occupant, was fatally injured. The ELT activated; the helicopter was substantially damaged and there was no post-impact fire. The TSB Edmonton office deployed investigators to the site.

C-GYSJ, a Central Mountain Air Ltd. de Havilland Aircraft of Canada DHC-8-102 (Dash 8) was preparing to conduct flight GLR9316, under instrument flight rules, from Port Hardy Airport (CYZT), BC, to Vancouver International Airport (CYVR), BC, with 3 crewmembers on board. At 1730 Pacific Daylight Time (PDT), while on the apron in CYZT, the crew attempted to start the aircraft auxiliary power unit (APU). The start was unsuccessful, and the APU along with the aircraft batteries were cycled off prior to attempting a second start. During the second start attempt, ground crew observed black smoke coming from the tail section of the aircraft and informed the flight crew. A flight crew member exited the aircraft to visually observe the smoke and the crew concluded that they were experiencing an APU fire. The APU fault light inside the cockpit was illuminated, but the APU fire warning light was not. Manual discharge of the APU fire bottle was accomplished, and the fire department was called. Fire crews found high temperatures in the APU compartment but determined no further extinguishing agents were required.A maintenance inspection found no signs of fire within the APU but did find evidence of an APU generator overheat, along with damage to the APU generator. The APU generator was repaired, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-GYJZ, a Jazz Aviation LP de Havilland Aircraft of Canada DHC-8-402 (Dash 8 Q400), was preparing to conduct flight JZA416 under instrument flight rules from Vancouver International Airport (CYVR), BC, to Penticton Airport (CYYF), BC, with 4 crew members and 20 passengers on board. Prior to pushback, cabin crew reportedly detected the smell of electrical smoke. While investigating the source of the fumes, a passenger approached a cabin crew member with an external battery that showed signs of being abnormally hot. The external battery was placed inside a lithium-ion battery incident kit (LIBIK). The LIBIK containing the battery was removed from the aircraft and retrieved by fire crews for disposal of the battery inside. Prior to departure, the empty LIBIK was returned to the aircraft. There were no injuries, and no damage to the aircraft was reported.

C-GTVL, Bell 206-B3 helicopter, operated by Quantum Helicopters, was conducting a local animal survey flight, under visual flight rules, from Williams Lake Airport (CYWL), BC. While flying at approximately 9 300 feet above sea level (ASL) the pilot heard a loud bang and the helicopter yawed. The engine (Rolls Royce Allison 250-C20B) indications showed that the engine had lost power. Concurrently, there was smoke in the cockpit, a warning horn, and the engine chip warning illuminated. The pilot broadcast a MAYDAY call and turned on the emergency locator transmitter (ELT). The pilot executed a successful autorotation and landed in a meadow at approximately       6 800 feet ASL. Once the pilot and passengers egressed, the pilot used the satellite phone to contact the British Columbia Wildfire Service (BCWFS). The BCWFS dispatched 2 helicopters to recover the pilot and passengers and relayed to the Joint Rescue and Coordination Centre that the pilot was turning off the ELT and that further support was not required. There were no injuries, and the helicopter was not damaged.The helicopter was airlifted from the landing site, and it was determined that the engine failure may have initiated at the top mounting structure at the exhaust collector. Internal engine damage was consistent with the turbine being out of alignment and there were indications of blade rub. The engine was sent for further examination.

C-FTHD, a Summit Helicopters Limited Bell 407 departed Kamloops Airport (CYKA), BC, under visual flight rules for a local training flight with 3 crew members on board. While in a low hover practicing fire suppression using a long line and a water bucket, the trainee pilot inadvertently selected the hook release instead of water release and inadvertently dropped the bucket and long line from approximately 15-20' feet above ground level. There were no injuries; the helicopter was not damaged.

C-GRSX, a privately registered Cessna 305A (L-19 Bird Dog) was operating on a cross-country flight from a private airstrip 15 NM E of Peace River, AB, to Red Deer Regional Airport (CYQF), AB. An en-route stop was planned at Valleyview Aerodrome (CEL5), AB. While touching down on Runway 25 at CEL5, the aircraft began to drift to the left. The pilot was unable to regain control and the aircraft departed the left edge of the runway. While the left main landing gear transitioned from the paved runway surface to the grass, the aircraft began to ground loop. Subsequently the right main landing gear collapsed, and the right wing contacted the ground and fractured as the aircraft came to rest. The pilot, who was the sole occupant, was uninjured.

C-FWSI, a Boeing 737 operated by WestJet Airlines was conducting flight WJA145 from Calgary Intl., AB (CYYC) to Fort McMurray, AB (CYMM). N103RM, a Cessna T310 was conducting a night VFR forest fire mapping flight southwest of the Fort McMurray Airport, AB (CYMM). During the RNAV Y approach into CYMM, the flight crew of WJA145 was made aware of VFR traffic in the vicinity of CYMM by ATS. The pilot of N103RM was operating outside of the CYMM control zone and monitoring 126.7 MHz. However, ATS was unable to make any radio contact with N103RM on any of the designated frequencies. Approximately 11 nm SW of CYMM, WJA154 took evasive action to avoid traffic by performing a right hand race track pattern before continuing the approach for an uneventful landing in CYMM.Separation was reduced to 2.3 nm laterally and 200' vertically, when 3 nm laterally or 1000' vertically are required.

C-FNWD, a WestJet Boeing 737-8 (Max 8) departed Tampa International Airport (KTPA), FL, as flight WJA1285, under instrument flight rules, to Vancouver International Airport (CYVR), BC. Shortly after arriving at the gate at CYVR, the flight crew was alerted by the ground crew to the presence of flames coming from the number one engine (CFM International LEAP 1B27). The flight crew was unable to visually verify the engine fire due to the passenger boarding bridge blocking their view. The flight crew checked the cockpit for indications of an engine fire. The cabin crew, having been made aware of the fire, initiated evacuation procedures to get the passengers off the plane after receiving confirmation from the flight crew. The flight crew gave the order to evacuate through the aircraft’s public address system and conducted the Engine Fire on Ground checklist and the Evacuation checklist. As part of the first checklist, the aircraft’s left engine halon fire suppression system was activated. Sixty-five passengers egressed the aircraft using the passenger boarding bridge while the remaining fifty-six passengers egressed the aircraft using the rear emergency slides located at the rear aircraft doors. Aircraft rescue and firefighting crews were dispatched to the scene and inspected the aircraft; however, the tail pipe flame had extinguished prior to their arrival. There were no reported injuries. There was no damage to the aircraft.Maintenance found that the center vent tube extension (CVTE) had a significant amount of oil coking which caused the oil to pool in the exhaust nozzle. The pooled oil ignited after the engines were shut down due to the heat in the exhaust cone and this created the tail pipe fire. An inspection for engine exposure to fire and extinguishing agents was carried out successfully. The CVTE, exhaust tube support, and injection nozzle were all removed and cleaned. The CVTE extension was replaced. The rear aircraft emergency slides were replaced as was the left engine halon fire bottle. The aircraft was returned to service.

C-GCGB, an Airspan Helicopters Ltd. Bell 212, was transporting wildfire crews near Bison Lake, AB, approximately 49 nm ENE of Manning Airport (CFX4), AB. While transiting to a fire suppression area NE of Bison Lake the pilot observed a 'TRANS OIL PRESSURE' light accompanied by a drop in transmission oil pressure. The pilot reduced power and landed immediately and shut down the aircraft. The pilot and passengers disembarked the aircraft without further incident.Following the flight the maintenance team found a ruptured transmission oil line. The line was replaced, and the aircraft was returned to service.

C-FMFD, a privately registered Piper PA-18-150, was conducting a VFR flight near Stormer Lake, ON, to Red Lake (Howey Bay) Water Aerodrome (CKS4), ON. While enroute, the airplane was flying at approximately 500 feet above ground level and slowed to an estimated 70 miles per hour at an idle power setting, over a lodge near Stormer Lake to observe damage conditions of the area from a recent forest fire. When power was applied to regain airspeed, the inability to move the throttle from its idle position was reported. The airplane was unable to maintain altitude and struck terrain. There were no injuries, and the airplane was substantially damaged.  After the accident, a maintenance facility inspected the function of the throttle linkage and found it to move freely.

C-GZNR, an Airbus Helicopters AS350 B3e operated by the Nova Scotia Department of Natural Resources and Renewables, was conducting aerial fire suppression operations near Five Finger Lake, NS (44°40'26"N, 065°11'19"W). While refilling the water bucket from the lake and beginning to lift off with the load at approximately 75 feet above the lake surface, the pilot reported hearing a loud bang followed by a loss of power. The helicopter subsequently impacted the water and became partially submerged. The pilot sustained serious injuries and was transported to hospital for medical treatment. The TSB is investigating.

C-FSHC, a Sierra Helicopters Aerospatiale AS 350 B-2 departed Squamish Municipal Airfield (Don Patrick Field)(CYSE), BC, on a British Columbia Wildfire Services (BCWS) tasking, to a fire on Mount (Mt) Currie under visual flight rules with 1 pilot and 3 passengers on board. The 3 passengers on board were an initial action firefighting crew deploying to fight the fire on Mt Currie. The pilot gave a safety briefing, and the crew lead a hover exit walk through prior to takeoff. The pilot and the crew lead were in the front seats, and the other two members were in the rear left and rear center seat. The equipment was strapped in the rear right seat. The drop off location was a steep talus field on the northern face of Mt Currie. The pilot and crew lead agreed on a large flat rock for the drop off position. The pilot did an overhead recce and completed an approach to the rock. He repositioned once for a more stable position and had the toe of both skids resting on the rock. The crew member in the left rear seat removed his headset, put on a hardhat, and exited the aircraft. The second crew member in the back removed his seatbelt and headset, put on his hardhat, and began passing equipment to the outside member in packages that were less than 20lbs. All crew members heard a sharp noise, and the aircraft pitched nose high and to the left. The outside person leapt down and away from the aircraft. The helicopter turned 180° and rolled down the slope. During the roll down the slope, the crew member in the back seat was ejected from the helicopter and the pilot's helmet came off. The helicopter came to rest in an upright, nose down attitude. The pilot and passenger were both able to exit the aircraft prior to the airframe being engulfed in flame. The crew member who had been outside the aircraft called a Mayday on his handheld radio and started downhill toward the wreckage. The four members grouped together and started to climb back up the slope, away from the burning helicopter. The crew lead used his cell phone to call in to dispatch and advise the status of the helicopter and crew. A BCWS team was dispatched for the rescue and recovered the crew to the Pemberton Aerodrome (CYPS), BC. All four occupants had minor injuries. The helicopter was destroyed.

N347CM, a Boeing 767-323 aircraft operated by Amerijet International Airlines, was conducting flight AJT8620 from Brussels International Airport (EBBR), Belgium, to Gander International Airport (CYQX), NL. During the landing rollout on Runway 13 at CYQX, smoke began accumulating in the cockpit. The crew brought the aircraft to a full stop before reaching the intersection of Runway 03/21 and donned their oxygen masks. The crew then received a forward cargo fire warning, followed by an aft cargo fire warning. The crew declared a MAYDAY, requested emergency rescue services (ERS), and began the quick reference handbook procedures for fire indications and smoke removal. The fire suppression systems were discharged, and the smoke and the fire warnings were cleared. Following an exterior inspection by ERS the crew continued to use oxygen and taxied to the apron to shut down. The crew received medical assessment by first responders and were also given a detailed medical examination at the local hospital before being released.The subsequent inspection of cargo and cargo hold areas revealed no sign of fire.

C-GDDR, a WestJet Boeing 737-8 was operating flight WJA65 from Glasgow International Airport (EGPF), Scotland, to Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport (CYYZ), ON. With about 3 hours remaining in the flight, all 4 flight attendants (FA) experienced shortness of breath due to fumes detected in the aft cabin. Two passengers in the aft cabin experienced similar symptoms. The flight crew contacted MediLink before deciding to divert to Goose Bay Airport (CYYR), NL, which was about 113 NM southeast of their position. The FA maintained their safety related duties and the aircraft landed at CYYR without incident where ATC had deployed emergency services to meet the aircraft. The crew and passengers were assessed by paramedics and released. Fire crews inspected the aircraft for the source of the fumes and tested the air quality in the aircraft. Maintenance personnel identified the source of the fumes as a faulty aft galley oven.

C-GGMZ, a Jazz Aviation DHC-8-402 (Dash 8 Q400), was being operated as flight JZA366 from Fort St. John Airport (CYXJ), BC, under instrument flight rules, to Vancouver International Airport (CYVR), BC. After retracting the landing gear after takeoff, the flight crew noticed the No.2 hydraulic fluid hot (HYD FLUID HOT), No.2 engine (Pratt & Whitney Canada, PW150A) hydraulic pump (ENG HYD PUMP), and the elevator pressure (ELEVATOR PRESS) caution lights illuminate. The hydraulic fluid level was observed to have dropped to 40%. The flight crew actioned the quick reference handbook, spoke with company maintenance, and planned to continue to CYVR. Approximately 8 minutes south of Prince George Airport (CYXS), BC, the flight crew noticed the hydraulic fluid level had dropped to 35%. They decided to divert to CYXS, declared an emergency, and landed safely on Runway 33. The flight crew stopped the aircraft on the runway, set the park brakes, and feathered both propellers. Fire trucks inspected the aircraft and could not see any visible signs of a fluid leak. The flight crew decided to taxi to the ramp. After the aircraft was parked on the ramp and as the passengers were deplaning, the fire crews noticed that there was hydraulic fluid on the ground underneath the No.2 engine. The flight crew confirmed the hydraulic leak. There were no reported injuries or damage to the aircraft.Maintenance personnel found the hydraulic fluid leak was coming from the No.2 hydraulic engine-driven pump (EDP). The EDP was replaced and flushing carried out. All associated filters were also replaced. The aircraft was returned to service. Reference SDR 20260805006.
